title: Access-A-Ride in NYC: how to qualify, book and pay
seoTitle: Access-A-Ride NYC: Eligibility, Booking and Fares
seoDesc: How Access-A-Ride paratransit works in New York City: who qualifies, the free assessment, booking by phone or MY AAR, the fare, e-hail, and options outside NYC.
dek: Access-A-Ride is the MTA's shared-ride service for New Yorkers whose disability keeps them off buses and subways. Here is how to apply, book a trip and pay, plus what's available outside the city.
keyFacts: Runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, across all five boroughs
Fare equals the full subway and bus fare ($3); a listed care attendant rides free
Book 1 to 2 days ahead, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.: 877-337-2017, option 2
Eligibility decision within 21 days of your in-person assessment
Cancel at least two hours before pickup
body:
Access-A-Ride (AAR) is the MTA's paratransit service for New York City residents and visitors whose disability prevents them from using public buses and subways. You apply, go to a free in-person assessment, and if approved, book shared rides a day or two ahead for the same fare as a subway ride.

Age alone doesn't qualify someone. A healthy 80-year-old who can ride the bus won't be approved, while a 66-year-old with severe arthritis who can't manage stairs might be. This guide covers who qualifies, how to apply, how to book and pay, the e-hail pilot, and what's available outside the city.

Who qualifies for Access-A-Ride?

Access-A-Ride follows the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). It serves people whose disability prevents them from using buses and subways, some or all of the time. After the assessment, the MTA assigns one of these eligibility types.

Eligibility typeWhat it means
FullEligible for all trips
Temporary fullEligible for all trips for a limited time
ConditionalEligible only in certain conditions
Temporary conditionalConditional eligibility for a limited time
ContinualOngoing eligibility with no recertification, though an update form is due every 5 years
IneligibleDoes not meet the criteria

Conditional eligibility covers specific barriers. Examples include inaccessible subway stations, extreme cold (a forecast of 39°F or below), extreme heat (a forecast of 90°F or above), unfamiliar places, or a stop or station more than a set number of blocks away.

The service area is all five boroughs plus a three-quarter-mile band beyond the city line into nearby parts of Nassau and Westchester counties. It runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays.

How do you apply?

  1. Submit an inquiry. Use the online inquiry form linked from the MTA's apply page or call 877-337-2017 and choose option 4 for eligibility (9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday to Friday).
  2. Get your packet. The MTA mails a paper application, an appointment letter and instructions for booking free round-trip transportation to the assessment.
  3. Book your ride to the assessment. It's free. Mention if a personal care attendant (PCA) will travel with you. PCAs ride free too.
  4. Bring the completed application. Assessments are held at centers in each borough, based on availability.
  5. Meet with a health care professional. The assessment includes an interview and, if appropriate, functional testing.
  6. Wait for the decision. The MTA decides within 21 days of the assessment and mails your eligibility letter.

If your parent is denied or given only conditional eligibility, they can appeal within 60 days. The appeal form and instructions come with the eligibility letter.

Full and conditional riders recertify every 5 years. If you don't get a recertification notice, contact the Eligibility Unit about six weeks before the AAR ID expires.

Helping a parent apply

Go with your mom or dad to the assessment if you can. Bring a list of medications and conditions, and be ready to describe a bad day as well as a good one. People tend to downplay their limits when a stranger is watching.

How do you book a trip?

Trips are booked one to two days in advance. Same-day trips are not available.

  • By phone. Call 877-337-2017 from the New York area, or 718-393-4999 from elsewhere. Choose your language, then option 2. Agents take reservations 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., seven days a week.
  • Online or in the app. Use MY AAR (linked from the MTA's book and manage trips page) or the MTA app, logging in with your AAR ID and password. First-time users register first.
  • By text. Send any text to 833-227-6928 to start a text session with AAR.
  • Relay. Customers who are deaf or hard of hearing can use their preferred relay service or 711.

Other phone options

On the same lines, option 1 is a 24/7 self-service system. Option 3 lets you check, cancel or ask for a later pickup on a trip booked for today, with agents available 24/7. Option 5 handles subscription service, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily. Option 6 takes feedback, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays.

Subscription trips and cancellations

If your parent goes from the same place to the same place at the same time at least once a week, such as dialysis or a day program, ask for a subscription trip. Request it at least three days before the first ride.

Cancel any trip at least two hours before pickup. To change a trip, cancel it and rebook with the new details. AAR is a shared-ride service, so trips may include other stops. Build extra time into appointments.

What does Access-A-Ride cost?

The Access-A-Ride fare matches the full subway and local bus fare, which is $3 as of the January 4, 2026 fare change. Each one-way trip is paid separately.

RiderFare
AAR customer$3, same as the full subway and bus fare
Personal care attendant noted on the AAR IDFree
Guest without the PCA notationFull AAR fare, in exact change
Fair Fares NYC participant paying with OMNYHalf fare

There are two ways to pay. Pay the driver in exact change, since drivers don't give change. Or preload money on the AAR OMNY ID card. AAR vehicles have no OMNY readers, so show the card to the driver and the fare comes off your balance at the end of the trip. Eligible customers get the AAR OMNY ID card by mail, and it also works as photo ID. It can't be used for taxi or e-hail trips.

Four free rides a day on buses and subways

Eligible AAR customers also get four free rides a day on MTA subways, local, limited and Select Bus Service buses, the Staten Island Railway and the Roosevelt Island Tram. For a parent who can manage some trips on transit, that's a real saving.

On good days, the bus or subway may be faster, and for AAR riders the first four rides each day are free.

What is the e-hail pilot?

The MTA's E-Hail Pilot Program gives some AAR customers on-demand rides through taxi and app services. It has run since 2017. Participants were selected at random, and the MTA says it is not adding customers on request.

  • The rider pays $4 per trip to start.
  • The MTA covers up to $60 of each trip, so a trip costing up to $64 costs the rider $4. The rider pays anything above that.
  • Each participant gets 25 or 40 subsidized trips per calendar month, based on past use. After that, the rider pays the full cost.
  • Providers are Arro, CTG, Lyft, Uber and the Drivers Cooperative. CTG, Uber and the Drivers Cooperative also take phone bookings.

If your parent wasn't chosen, the regular advance-booking service is the option. The MTA's page describes the current phase as starting in July 2024, so check the MTA e-hail page for the latest terms.

What mistakes trip people up?

  • Waiting until the day of. Same-day trips aren't available. Book one to two days ahead, between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m.
  • Cancelling too late. Cancel at least two hours before pickup. MY AAR and the 24/7 same-day line (option 3) make this easier, even at night.
  • Bringing the wrong money. Drivers don't make change. Carry the exact fare or keep money on the AAR OMNY ID card.
  • Bringing a helper who isn't listed. A companion rides free only if "PCA" is noted on the AAR ID. Otherwise they pay the full fare as a guest.
  • Letting eligibility lapse. Watch for the recertification notice. If it doesn't come, call the Eligibility Unit about six weeks before the ID expires.
  • Not appealing. If a denial or conditional rating doesn't match your parent's real limits, appeal within 60 days.

What about visitors and riders outside NYC?

Visitors who are paratransit-eligible where they live can use AAR for up to 21 days in a 365-day period. Contact the AAR Eligibility Unit at least 2 weeks before arriving. Documents can be faxed to 718-393-4306 or mailed to AAR Eligibility, Department of Paratransit, 130 Livingston Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201.

Outside the five boroughs and the border band, paratransit is run by local systems. In Nassau County it's NICE Able-Ride (reservations 516-228-4000). In Suffolk County it's Suffolk County Accessible Transit, or SCAT (631-853-8337). The MTA's paratransit providers page also lists services in Westchester, Rockland, Putnam, Orange and Dutchess counties. Upstate and elsewhere, ask your county's transit agency or Office for the Aging. NY Connects can point you to the right office at 1-800-342-9871.

Should your parent also get a Reduced-Fare card?

Yes, if they're 65 or older and ride buses or subways at all. MTA reduced fare is $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare. It's a separate program from Access-A-Ride, and there's no assessment for riders 65 and up. See our guide to MTA reduced fare in New York for how to apply.

If your parent recently stopped driving or just came home from rehab, it can help to set up both at once. Our caregiver support guide lists other help for families managing a parent's appointments.

faq.q: How do I sign my mom up for Access-A-Ride in Queens?
faq.a: Start with the MTA's online inquiry form (aar.mta.info/inquiry) or call 877-337-2017 and choose option 4. The MTA mails an application and an appointment for a free in-person assessment, with free round-trip transportation. A decision comes within 21 days of the assessment.

faq.q: Does my dad in Staten Island qualify for Access-A-Ride just because he's over 65?
faq.a: No. Access-A-Ride is based on disability, and age alone doesn't qualify anyone. He qualifies if a disability keeps him from using buses and subways some or all of the time. At 65 he does qualify for MTA reduced fare, which is a separate program.

faq.q: How much is an Access-A-Ride trip?
faq.a: The fare matches the full subway and bus fare, $3. A personal care attendant listed on the AAR ID rides free. Guests pay the full fare in exact change.

faq.q: Can I book Access-A-Ride for the same day?
faq.a: No. Trips are booked one to two days in advance, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., by calling 877-337-2017 (option 2) or through MY AAR or the MTA app.

faq.q: Does Access-A-Ride go to Long Island or Westchester?
faq.a: Only a short way. The service area includes a three-quarter-mile band beyond the city line into nearby parts of Nassau and Westchester. Beyond that, local paratransit applies, such as NICE Able-Ride in Nassau (516-228-4000) or SCAT in Suffolk (631-853-8337).

faq.q: How do I cancel an Access-A-Ride trip?
faq.a: Cancel at least two hours before pickup through MY AAR or the MTA app, or call 877-337-2017. Choose option 2 for trips booked 1 to 2 days out (7 a.m. to 5 p.m.) or option 3 for a trip today (24/7).

title: New York estate tax: the 2026 exclusion, the cliff and filing
seoTitle: New York Estate Tax 2026: $7.35M Exclusion and Cliff
seoDesc: New York's 2026 estate tax exclusion is $7,350,000. How the 105% cliff works, who files Form ET-706, the nine-month deadline and the three-year gift add-back.
dek: Most New York estates owe no state estate tax, but the ones near the line need to plan carefully. Here is the 2026 exclusion amount, the cliff, and what an executor must file.
keyFacts: 2026 basic exclusion amount: $7,350,000 (deaths Jan 1 to Dec 31, 2026)
2025 basic exclusion amount: $7,160,000
No credit at all once the taxable estate tops 105% of the exclusion
File Form ET-706 and pay within nine months of death
Taxable gifts made within three years of death are added back
body:
New York's estate tax applies only when an estate is larger than the basic exclusion amount, which is $7,350,000 for people who die in 2026. Above that line the tax rises fast, and once the taxable estate passes 105% of the exclusion, tax is figured on the whole taxable estate.

That sharp jump is what planners call the New York cliff. Most families will never come close to it. But estates with a paid-off house in the city or suburbs, retirement accounts and life insurance can add up faster than people expect. This guide explains the numbers, who files, and the gift rule that surprises many families.

What is the 2026 exclusion amount?

The basic exclusion amount is the value an estate can have before New York estate tax applies. The New York State Department of Taxation and Finance publishes it by date of death.

Date of deathBasic exclusion amount
January 1 to December 31, 2026$7,350,000
January 1 to December 31, 2025$7,160,000
2027Not yet published by the Tax Department

The amount is adjusted for inflation each year. As of late November 2026, the Tax Department had not posted the 2027 figure. Check the Tax Department's estate tax page for updates.

The federal estate tax is a separate tax with its own exemption and rules.

How does the New York cliff work?

New York gives every estate a credit that wipes out the tax on estates at or below the exclusion amount. Above the exclusion, that credit shrinks quickly. When the taxable estate is more than 105% of the exclusion, the credit disappears entirely, and tax is figured on the full taxable estate.

The 105% line comes straight from the Tax Department's rule. Its Form ET-706 instructions for 2025 deaths put the cutoff at $7,518,000, which is 105% of that year's $7,160,000 exclusion. Applying the same 105% rule to the 2026 exclusion of $7,350,000 gives $7,717,500. So for 2026 deaths the credit phases out between $7,350,000 and $7,717,500, and above $7,717,500 there's no credit at all.

An example

Say your mother dies in 2026 with a taxable estate of $7,300,000. That's under the exclusion, so no New York estate tax is due. Now say it's $7,800,000. That's above $7,717,500, so the credit is gone and tax is figured on the entire $7,800,000. Going over the line by a few hundred thousand dollars brings tax on the full amount.

Date of deathExclusion amountNo credit above (105% of exclusion)
2026$7,350,000$7,717,500
2025$7,160,000$7,518,000

That's why the last few hundred thousand dollars matter so much in New York. Planners sometimes use charitable gifts in a will to bring an estate back under the line, since a smaller tax bill can leave heirs with more. Ask an estate lawyer or accountant about this if an estate is anywhere near the cliff.

Near the line, a modest charitable bequest can sometimes leave the family with more money in the end.

Who has to file a New York estate tax return?

The executor files. The rules differ for residents and nonresidents.

  • New York residents. File if the federal gross estate plus includible gifts is more than the basic exclusion amount.
  • Nonresidents. File if the estate includes real estate or tangible property located in New York, and the same total is more than the exclusion amount. A Florida retiree who kept a house in the Hudson Valley is a common example.

The return is Form ET-706. Use the version that matches the date of death. A completed federal Form 706 must be filed with it, even when the estate doesn't have to file a federal return.

  1. Value everything at date of death. Include real estate, accounts, retirement plans, life insurance the decedent owned, business interests and personal property.
  2. Add back recent gifts. Include taxable gifts made in the three years before death that are not already in the estate (see below).
  3. Compare to the exclusion. If the total is over the exclusion amount for the year of death, the estate must file.
  4. Prepare ET-706 and federal Form 706. Use the ET-706 version for the date of death. Attach the completed federal return.
  5. File and pay within nine months of death. If you need more time, request an extension on Form ET-133.
  6. Clear the lien on real estate. To sell or transfer New York real estate, you may need a Release of Lien of Estate Tax (Form ET-117) for each county where it's located. Estates that don't need to file ET-706 use Form ET-30 to apply for the release.

What is the three-year gift add-back?

Giving money away shortly before death doesn't automatically reduce a New York estate. For New York residents, taxable gifts made within three years of death are added back to the estate if they aren't already included in the federal gross estate. A taxable gift here means a gift that would be taxable under section 2503 of the Internal Revenue Code.

A few gifts are not added back.

  • Gifts made while the person was not a New York resident.
  • Gifts made before April 1, 2014.
  • Gifts made between January 1 and January 15, 2019.
  • Gifts of real or tangible property located outside New York when the gift was made.

Here's how it plays out. Say your father, a New York resident, gave his daughter $500,000 toward a home in 2025 and died in 2026. If that gift was taxable under federal gift rules and isn't already in his federal gross estate, the taxable part is added back when figuring whether his estate crosses $7,350,000 and how much New York tax is due.

In practice, this means deathbed gifting rarely helps with New York tax. Gifts made well before the three-year window are a different matter, which is one reason estate plans work best when they start early.

What counts toward the estate?

The starting point is the federal gross estate, the same figure used on federal Form 706. It generally includes what the person owned at death, valued as of the date of death. For most New York families the big pieces are the home, bank and brokerage accounts, retirement accounts and any life insurance the person owned.

Real estate is often the surprise. A house bought decades ago in Westchester, on Long Island or in Brooklyn may now be worth far more than the family thinks. Get a realistic value before deciding the estate is safely under the line. For an estate near the exclusion, a formal appraisal is worth the cost, because the cliff turns small valuation differences into large tax differences.

When is the tax due, and can you get more time?

The executor must file the New York return, the federal return and pay any tax due within nine months of the date of death. An extension to file or pay is requested on Form ET-133. Extensions generally can't be longer than six months, though the Tax Department may allow up to four years to pay in cases of undue hardship.

Estimate the tax early. If the estate is short on cash because most of its value is in a house, talk to a tax professional well before the nine-month mark.

Who pays the tax, the estate or the heirs?

New York's tax is charged on the estate itself. The executor files and pays it from the estate before heirs receive their shares. The Tax Department's instructions direct the executor to file the return and pay the tax.

Families split between states should check the other state's rules too, because each state sets its own death taxes. If a parent lived in New Jersey or another state but owned a house or land in New York, the nonresident filing rule above applies on the New York side.

Income tax is a separate question from estate tax. Our guide to how New York taxes retirement income covers the state income tax side for older adults.

Who should the executor call first?

Start with the estate's lawyer or accountant, and do it in the first month or two. The ET-706 needs a completed federal Form 706 attached, and that return takes time to prepare. Appraisals of real estate and business interests take time too. Starting early leaves room to ask for an extension on Form ET-133 if it's needed.

What should families do now?

Add up the rough value of your parent's estate, including the house, retirement accounts and any life insurance they own. If the total is well under $7 million, New York estate tax is unlikely to be a worry, though the rest of their plan still matters. Our guides to powers of attorney and probate in New York cover the paperwork every family needs.

If the total is in the $6 million to $8 million range, or growing, see an estate planning lawyer or CPA. The cliff makes small differences expensive, and the three-year add-back rules out last-minute fixes.

faq.q: What is the New York estate tax exemption for 2026?
faq.a: The basic exclusion amount is $7,350,000 for dates of death from January 1 through December 31, 2026. For 2025 deaths it was $7,160,000.

faq.q: What is the 2027 New York estate tax exclusion?
faq.a: As of late November 2026, the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance had not published the 2027 amount. Check tax.ny.gov for the update.

faq.q: Will my parents' house in Nassau County push their estate over the New York limit?
faq.a: Add the house's value to their bank and retirement accounts, life insurance they own and other assets. If the total for a 2026 death is more than $7,350,000, the estate must file Form ET-706. Above $7,717,500 (105% of the exclusion), tax applies to the whole taxable estate.

faq.q: My dad lived in Florida but owned a cabin in the Adirondacks. Does his estate owe New York tax?
faq.a: A nonresident's estate must file if it includes New York real estate or tangible property and the federal gross estate plus includible gifts is more than the exclusion amount. The Form ET-706 instructions explain how a nonresident estate's tax is figured, so ask the estate's accountant to work through them.

faq.q: When is the New York estate tax return due?
faq.a: Form ET-706, along with a completed federal Form 706, and any tax due must be filed and paid within nine months of the date of death. Extensions are requested on Form ET-133.

faq.q: Can my mom give money away to avoid New York estate tax?
faq.a: Taxable gifts made within three years of death are generally added back to a New York resident's estate. Gifts made earlier are not added back, so planning ahead matters. Talk to an estate planning lawyer before making large gifts.

title: Funeral and burial costs in New York: your rights and the help
seoTitle: Funeral and Burial Costs in New York: Rights and Help
seoDesc: Funeral costs and rights in New York: the price list you're owed, prepaid funerals and Medicaid, Social Security's $255, VA burial pay and NYC's HRA allowance.
dek: A funeral is one of the biggest purchases a family makes, usually in a day or two and in grief. Here is what New York and federal law say you're owed, how prepaid plans work, and where help with the bill comes from.
keyFacts: Funeral homes must give prices by phone and a General Price List you can keep
You can supply your own casket or urn with no handling fee
Social Security's one-time death payment is $255
NYC HRA burial allowance: up to $1,700; apply within 120 days of death
VA, death on or after Oct 1, 2026: $1,032 burial plus $1,032 plot, if VA rules are met
body:
In New York, a funeral home has to give you prices over the phone and a written General Price List before you choose anything, and you only pay for what you pick. Help with the bill can come from Social Security, the VA, a prepaid funeral agreement, and for low-income families, the city or county.

The New York Attorney General's office says the average viewing, ceremony and burial in the state costs over $8,500, before the plot or cremation. Knowing your rights is the easiest way to keep that number in check.

What does a funeral home have to tell me about prices?

Federal and state rules both require written prices. The Federal Trade Commission's Funeral Rule and New York's own rules from the state Department of Health say you can buy each item separately and turn down a package.

  • Prices by phone. A funeral home must give you price information on the phone. Under the FTC rule, you don't have to give your name, address or number first.
  • A General Price List to keep. You get it at the start of the meeting, or when you stop in to ask. You don't have to buy anything to get it.
  • A casket price list before you see caskets. The same goes for vaults and grave liners. Ask about lower-priced items that aren't on display.
  • An itemized statement before you pay. It lists each item, its price and the total. In New York this statement usually serves as your contract.

What can't they charge for?

New York's Department of Health lists charges that are illegal for funeral homes. They include a fee for filing the death certificate, a handling fee for paying outside vendors for you, a fee for handling a casket you bought elsewhere, and any charge for something you didn't choose. Staff may not pressure you or criticize the items you pick.

A few more rules help families most.

  • Embalming isn't required by state law. The funeral home needs your approval to embalm. It may require embalming for some choices, such as an open-casket viewing.
  • No casket is required for cremation. You can use an alternative container made of cardboard, pressed wood, composition materials or canvas.
  • Bring your own casket or urn. One bought online or from a local seller must be accepted with no extra fee.
  • Cash advance items at cost. Cemetery fees, death certificates and clergy are paid to others, and the funeral home can't profit on them.
  • You can switch funeral homes. You pay for work already done, but the home can't hold the body until you pay.
Call two or three funeral homes and ask for the same thing, such as a direct cremation. The phone call costs nothing and the law says they have to answer.

What are the main costs, and which can we skip?

The General Price List breaks a funeral into parts. The one charge you can't decline is the basic arrangements fee. It covers having a funeral director, staff and equipment ready to respond to a death.

ItemCan you decline it?
Basic arrangements feeNo. It is already built into direct burial and direct cremation prices.
EmbalmingYes, unless your choices require it, such as a public viewing
RefrigerationYes. If charged, it must be on the price list.
CasketNot required by state law, though many cemeteries require a suitable container. You may buy one elsewhere.
Vault or grave linerNot required by state law, though some cemeteries require one
Viewing, ceremony, hearse, flowersYes
Cemetery plot, opening and closing, crematory feeCharged by the cemetery or crematory, often on top of the funeral home bill

The lowest-cost choices are direct burial and direct cremation, according to the Department of Health. A direct burial includes a graveside ceremony if you want one. The Attorney General's office warns that the "direct cremation" price on a price list may not include the crematory's own fee, so ask for the full total.

If you choose cremation, the form you sign (the Customer's Designation of Intentions) has a space for what will happen to the ashes, and you get a copy. After 120 days, the funeral home may dispose of ashes nobody has claimed.

How do prepaid funerals work in New York?

New York lets you prepay a funeral through a pre-need agreement with a funeral home. The money stays yours. The funeral director must deposit it within 10 days in an interest-bearing account or a government-backed investment, and tell you within 30 days where it went.

Before you sign, the funeral director must give you a General Price List, a Pre-Need Itemization Statement and the Pre-Need Agreement itself. The agreement says whether the funeral is guaranteed or non-guaranteed.

  • Guaranteed. The money in the account covers the items you picked, even if prices go up. Cash advance items like cemetery fees and death certificates are usually left out.
  • Non-guaranteed. You pay prices at the time of the funeral. Any shortfall comes from the estate, and any extra goes back to it.

A revocable agreement can be cancelled at any time for the principal and interest, with no fees or penalties. If the funeral home is sold, both homes must tell you in writing within 30 days. To check whether a closed funeral home reported what it held, call the Department of Health's Bureau of Funeral Directing at 518-402-0785.

What changes if my parent is on Medicaid?

If your mom or dad is applying for or receiving Medicaid or SSI, New York law requires the agreement to be irrevocable. Your parent can never get the money back, though they can still move it to a different funeral home. The home must transfer it within 10 days of a written request. Anything left after the funeral goes to the county.

The upside is that an irrevocable agreement doesn't count as a resource for Medicaid. The Department of Health says paying fair market value for it isn't treated as a transfer of assets. For applicants who are 65 or older, blind or disabled, Medicaid can also allow a separate burial fund of up to $1,500 ($3,000 for a couple) if the agreement covers less than that for items other than the burial space. A cemetery plot, vault or headstone bought outright also doesn't count.

The agreement should not include food, lodging or travel for family and guests. If it does, and the purchase falls in the five-year look-back for nursing home care, those costs count as a transfer of assets. Our Medicaid guide covers the resource rules.

Where can help with the bill come from?

Several programs pay part of the cost. None of them covers a full funeral on its own.

SourceAmountWho
Social Security lump-sum death payment$255, one timeUsually a surviving spouse; if none, some children
VA burial allowance, highest rate, for a death on or after Sept. 11, 2001Up to $2,000Eligible person who paid; VA decides which rate applies, and a death from a service-connected disability is one qualifying case
VA burial and plot allowance, death on or after Oct. 1, 2026$1,032 burial plus $1,032 for a plotVeteran must meet a VA condition, such as getting a VA pension or compensation, or dying in VA care
NYC HRA burial allowanceUp to $1,700Low-income NYC residents; total bill generally $3,400 or less
County Department of Social Services, outside NYCVaries by countyLow-income residents; call the county

How does the New York City burial allowance work?

HRA's Office of Burial Services pays up to $1,700 toward the funeral of a low-income New Yorker who died without resources or assets. A relative who is legally responsible must also be unable to pay. It can repay a bill you already paid or approve a planned funeral in advance. If the bill is over $3,400, the cost of the plot, grave opening or cremation is subtracted, and if what's left is under $3,400, the allowance can still be approved.

  1. Apply within 120 days of death. The person responsible for the arrangements applies online, or on paper with Form M-860W.
  2. Upload documents. Proof of low income can include SNAP, cash assistance or SSI. Notarized papers can be uploaded but the original must also be mailed.
  3. Give the funeral home your claim number. It also needs your parent's last name and date of death to send its invoice through HRA's portal.
  4. Track your case. Call the DSS OneNumber at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Paper applications go to NYC HRA Office of Burial Services, 33-28 Northern Blvd., 3rd Floor, Long Island City, NY 11101.

Outside the city, the Attorney General's office says low-income families can apply for burial help up to 120 days after a death through the county Department of Social Services. Call your county DSS for its rules.

What burial benefits do veterans get?

A veteran discharged under conditions other than dishonorable can usually be buried in a VA national cemetery at no cost. That includes the grave, opening and closing, perpetual care, a headstone or marker and a burial flag. A spouse can be buried in the same grave, with their name added to the headstone. The funeral home's own charges are still the family's to pay.

New York has several VA national cemeteries, including Calverton National Cemetery on Long Island and the Gerald B.H. Solomon Saratoga National Cemetery. To schedule a burial, the funeral director calls the National Cemetery Scheduling Office at 1-800-535-1117.

New York's first state-run veterans cemetery is the New York State Veterans Cemetery, Finger Lakes, at 6632 NY-96A in Romulus, Seneca County. The state Department of Veterans' Services runs it. The funeral home sends the discharge papers to the cemetery to confirm eligibility. For help with benefits, the department's advisors are at 1-888-838-7697.

For the VA burial allowance, apply online or by mail on VA Form 21P-530EZ. For a death that wasn't service-connected, file within two years of the burial, with some exceptions. A spouse already listed on the veteran's VA profile is paid a set amount automatically and doesn't need to file. For questions, call your VA regional office.

Who oversees cemeteries, and where do I complain?

Different agencies handle different parts of the bill. Funeral homes answer to the state Department of Health. Most cemeteries answer to the Department of State.

  • Funeral homes. File a complaint with the Department of Health's Bureau of Funeral Directing, 875 Central Avenue, Albany, NY 12206, using the form on its website. For illegal or deceptive practices, you can also call the Attorney General's office at 1-800-771-7755.
  • Cemeteries. The Department of State's Division of Cemeteries oversees about 1,700 not-for-profit cemeteries, including lot sales and service fees. Reach it through the contact forms on its website.
  • The cemetery deed. If the funeral director holds it, it must be returned within 7 days of the funeral unless you agreed otherwise. Keep it safe, because it's hard to replace.

For the paperwork that comes before and after the funeral, see our guides to what to do when a parent dies, probate in New York and health care proxies and MOLST.

faq.q: How do I get help paying for my mom's funeral in the Bronx?
faq.a: If she was a low-income city resident without money or assets to cover the funeral, apply to HRA's Office of Burial Services within 120 days of her death. It pays up to $1,700, and the total bill generally has to be $3,400 or less after certain costs are subtracted. Call 718-557-1399 for help.

faq.q: Can my dad prepay his funeral if he's applying for Medicaid in Westchester?
faq.a: Yes. New York requires a prepaid funeral agreement for a Medicaid applicant to be irrevocable. It then doesn't count as a resource, and paying fair market value isn't treated as a transfer. He may also keep a separate burial fund of up to $1,500 in some cases. Leftover money goes to the county.

faq.q: Do I have to buy the casket from the funeral home?
faq.a: No. Under the FTC Funeral Rule and New York rules, you can buy a casket or urn online or from a local seller. The funeral home must accept it and can't charge a handling fee.

faq.q: Is embalming required in New York?
faq.a: No. State law doesn't require it, and the funeral director needs your approval to embalm. A funeral home may require it for some choices, such as an open-casket viewing. Direct burial and direct cremation don't need it.

faq.q: How much does the VA pay toward a veteran's funeral?
faq.a: For a death on or after October 1, 2026, VA lists $1,032 for burial and $1,032 for a plot when the veteran met one of its conditions, such as getting a VA pension or dying in VA care. Its highest rate, for some deaths on or after September 11, 2001, is up to $2,000. Burial in a VA national cemetery is free for eligible veterans.

faq.q: Can I get my money back from a prepaid funeral in New York?
faq.a: If the agreement is revocable, yes, with interest and no fees or penalties. If it's irrevocable, which is required for Medicaid and SSI applicants, the money can't be refunded, but it can be moved to another funeral home.

title: Home safety changes in New York: grab bars, ramps and repair help
seoTitle: Home Modifications for Seniors in NY: Grants and Help
seoDesc: RESTORE, Access to Home, NYC Aging home modifications and weatherization help older New Yorkers pay for grab bars, ramps and repairs. Who qualifies and how.
dek: Grab bars, ramps and urgent repairs can keep a parent safely at home. Here are the New York programs that help pay, who qualifies, and the low-cost changes that prevent falls.
keyFacts: RESTORE: emergency repairs for homeowners 60+ up to 100% of area median income
Access to Home: accessibility changes up to 80% of area median income
You apply through a local town, county or nonprofit, not HCR
NYC Aging Home Modification Program: 212-602-4455
Weatherization is free for eligible owners and renters; seniors get priority
body:
New York has several programs that pay for grab bars, ramps, railings and urgent repairs so older adults can stay safely at home. The main state programs are RESTORE, for emergency repairs for homeowners 60 and older, and Access to Home, for accessibility changes for people with disabilities; you apply through a local nonprofit or town, never to the state directly.

New York City adds its own options, including NYC Aging's Older Adult Home Modification Program, which installs modifications at no cost after an occupational therapist visits. Your county Office for the Aging can point you to local handyman or minor repair help, and the Weatherization Assistance Program can fix drafty, cold homes for free if income qualifies. This guide covers who qualifies for each, what they pay for, and the simple changes that prevent falls.

Which New York programs help pay for home safety changes?

The right program depends on what needs fixing, whether your parent owns or rents, and where they live. Here is a quick comparison from the official program pages.

ProgramWho qualifiesWhat it coversHow to apply
RESTORE (HCR)Homeowners 60+ living in the home, income at or below 100% of area median incomeEmergency repairs and code violations that threaten health or safetyThrough a local program administrator (town, county or nonprofit)
Access to Home (HCR)People with a documented disability, income at or below 80% of area median income; owners or rentersRamps, lifts, handrails, wider doorways, roll-in showersThrough a local program administrator
Access to Home for Medicaid Members (HCR)Medicaid members with a disability, same income limitSame kinds of accessibility changesThrough a local program administrator
NYC Aging Older Adult Home Modification ProgramEligible older New Yorkers in the five boroughsNo-cost grab bars, handrails, raised toilet seats, shower chairs, lighting, temporary ramps, non-slip flooring212-602-4455
HPD HomeFix (NYC)Owners of 1 to 4 family homes, income up to 120% of area median incomeNo-interest, forgivable repair loans, including accessibility measures for seniorsCenter for NYC Neighborhoods, 646-513-3470
Weatherization Assistance Program (HCR)Households at or below 60% of state median income; owners and rentersInsulation, air sealing, heating repairs, windows and doors, at no costLocal weatherization provider

How does the RESTORE program work?

RESTORE pays for emergency repairs for homeowners 60 and older. New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) funds it, and local governments and nonprofits run it.

To qualify, HCR says your parent must own the home and live in it as a primary residence, be 60 or older, and have household income no higher than 100% of the area median income. The repair must fix a hazard or deficiency that poses an immediate threat to life, health or safety, or a code violation.

Rockland County's community development office, which runs RESTORE locally, lists common covered repairs. They include serious structural problems with floors, doorways and entry decks, leaking roofs, broken exterior doors and windows, deteriorated stairs, failed heating systems, plumbing and hot water, electrical hazards and accessibility modifications. It does not cover kitchen or bathroom remodels, landscaping, cosmetic work or new construction. Rockland also requires applicants to be current on property taxes and to carry homeowners insurance. The income chart on its page lists 100% of area median income as $118,800 for one person and $135,700 for two. Other counties have different limits.

Funding comes in rounds, so a local program can be open or closed. As of November 2026, Rockland's page says RESTORE is not accepting applications and will open again if more funding becomes available. Call 845-364-3939 to ask.

You can't apply to the state for RESTORE or Access to Home. The money goes through a local town, county or nonprofit.

What does Access to Home pay for?

Access to Home helps people with disabilities make their homes accessible, so they can stay there or come home instead of moving to a facility. HCR gives wheelchair ramps and lifts, handrails, doorway widening and roll-in showers as examples.

The person must have a documented substantial limitation caused by a disability, and household income at or below 80% of area median income. The limit is 120% for veterans certified by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs or the Department of Defense as entitled to disability payments for a wartime disability. Renters can qualify too, as long as the landlord isn't already required by law to make the changes. A separate version, Access to Home for Medicaid Members, serves people on Medicaid with the same income rule.

  1. Open HCR's local grants list. HCR posts a list of active grants by county, including RESTORE and Access to Home, on its "Grants Available Through Local Partners" page.
  2. Call the group serving your parent's area. Confirm the program is open and ask for the application and income limit.
  3. Gather documents. Expect proof of age, income, ownership or lease, and, for Access to Home, documentation of the disability.
  4. Schedule the inspection. The local administrator decides what work qualifies.
  5. Ask about other help. If no grant is open, HCR suggests contacting the town or a local housing nonprofit. Also call the county Office for the Aging.

What help is there in New York City?

NYC Aging runs the Older Adult Home Modification Program. A licensed occupational therapist visits the home, recommends changes, and a licensed contractor installs them at no cost to the older adult.

NYC Aging says modifications may include grab bars, handrails, raised toilet seats, shower chairs, better lighting, temporary ramps and non-slip flooring. It coordinates the assessment, the plan, the installation and a follow-up visit. For eligibility or to apply, call 212-602-4455 or email HomeMod@aging.nyc.gov.

Homeowners can also look at HPD's HomeFix program. It offers no-interest, forgivable loans for repairs to one to four family homes, up to $100,000 for a one-family home. Eligible repairs can include roofs, heating, plumbing, electrical work and accessibility measures to help seniors. HomeFix requires the home to be the owner's primary residence, no reverse mortgage, and household income no more than 120% of area median income, which HPD lists as $142,560 for one person and $162,840 for two. Condos and co-ops are not eligible. Call the Center for NYC Neighborhoods Homeowner Hub at 646-513-3470.

Renters in the city should start with the landlord, and with NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 for help.

What can my county Office for the Aging do?

Many county offices fund or refer to minor home repair and handyman programs. What exists depends on the county, so call and ask by name for "minor home repair" or "residential repair."

  • Rockland County. The Office for the Aging lists CHORE, minor home repairs for adults 60 and older or people with disabilities, sponsored by BRiDGES at 845-624-1366 ext. 139. See the Rockland County page.
  • Suffolk County. The Office for the Aging says each of the ten towns has a Residential Repair program for small jobs around the house. Participants pay for materials. Examples include Babylon 631-789-3309, Brookhaven 631-451-9092, Huntington 631-446-3721, Islip 631-224-5424 and Smithtown 631-360-7616. See the Suffolk County page.
  • Other counties. Find the local number on your county page, or call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.

In 2022, NYSOFA began training county case managers as Certified Aging-in-Place Specialists, so they can assess a home and recommend changes. If your parent needs in-home help too, ask about EISEP, and see our NY Connects guide.

Can weatherization make an older home safer and cheaper to heat?

Yes. The Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP) improves energy efficiency and fixes energy-related health and safety problems at no cost to eligible homeowners and renters.

HCR says households may qualify with income at or below 60% of state median income, and seniors get priority. If anyone in the home gets SSI, public assistance or HEAP, the household is automatically eligible. Work starts with an energy audit and can include air sealing, attic or wall insulation, heating system repair or replacement, efficient lighting and appliances, window and door repair, and small repairs needed for energy savings. Owners of rental buildings must contribute to the cost.

To apply, contact the weatherization provider for your county, listed in HCR's online provider directory. For general questions, the WAP central office is 518-474-5700. If heating bills are the bigger worry, see our HEAP guide.

What simple changes help prevent falls?

The New York State Department of Health says falls are the leading cause of injury deaths, hospitalizations and emergency visits among adults 65 and older, and that falls are preventable. Many of its home tips cost little or nothing.

  • Remove papers, books, clothes and shoes from stairs and walkways.
  • Remove small throw rugs, or use double-sided tape so they don't slip.
  • Keep items used often in cabinets that can be reached without a step stool.
  • Have grab bars put in next to the toilet and in the tub or shower.
  • Use non-slip mats in the tub and on shower floors.
  • Brighten the lighting, and hang light curtains or shades to cut glare.
  • Have handrails and lights put in on all staircases.
  • Wear shoes inside and out, and avoid going barefoot or wearing slippers without grip.

The Department of Health also advises a yearly eye exam, a yearly foot check, and a medicine review with a doctor or pharmacist, since some medicines cause dizziness. It supports free evidence-based classes, including Tai Chi for Arthritis and Fall Prevention, A Matter of Balance and Stepping On. To find one nearby, call 518-402-7900, or ask at a senior center.

After a fall or hospital stay

Ask the hospital or rehab team whether an occupational therapist can assess the home before discharge. Then call the programs above.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Paying a stranger up front. Several programs above, including NYC Aging and HomeFix, arrange their own licensed or approved contractors. Be wary of anyone who knocks on the door offering repairs.
  • Waiting for one program. Funding opens and closes. Apply where you can and keep a list of others to call.
  • Skipping the renter options. Access to Home and weatherization can help renters, not just owners.

If the home simply can't be made safe, see our senior housing guide for other options.

faq.q: How do I get grab bars installed for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call NYC Aging's Older Adult Home Modification Program at 212-602-4455 or email HomeMod@aging.nyc.gov. For eligible older adults, a licensed occupational therapist assesses the home and a licensed contractor installs changes such as grab bars, handrails and shower chairs at no cost.

faq.q: Is there help paying for a wheelchair ramp for my dad in Westchester?
faq.a: Possibly, through New York's Access to Home program, for people with a documented disability and household income at or below 80% of area median income. Check HCR's list of active local grants by county for a Westchester administrator, and call the county Department of Senior Programs and Services.

faq.q: Who qualifies for the RESTORE program in New York?
faq.a: Homeowners 60 and older who live in the home as their primary residence and have household income at or below 100% of the area median income. The repair must fix an emergency or code violation that threatens health or safety. Apply through a local program administrator, not HCR.

faq.q: Can renters get accessibility modifications in New York?
faq.a: Yes. Access to Home can assist rental units, as long as the landlord isn't already required by law to make the changes. Renters can also apply for free weatherization. In NYC, the NYC Aging Home Modification Program serves eligible older adults.

faq.q: Does weatherization cost anything for seniors in New York?
faq.a: No. HCR says there is no cost to eligible homeowners and renters. Households at or below 60% of state median income may qualify, seniors get priority, and anyone receiving SSI, public assistance or HEAP is automatically eligible. Owners of rental buildings pay part of the cost.

faq.q: What are the cheapest ways to prevent falls at home?
faq.a: The NYS Department of Health suggests clearing clutter from stairs and walkways, removing or taping down throw rugs, using non-slip mats in the tub, improving lighting, keeping everyday items within reach, and installing grab bars and stair handrails. It also recommends yearly eye exams and a medicine review.

title: Moving a parent between New Jersey and New York: what changes
seoTitle: Moving a Parent Between NJ and NY: Medicaid, Taxes, ID
seoDesc: Moving a parent between New Jersey and New York: Medicaid starts over, Medicare plan changes, property tax relief, license deadlines, voting and estate taxes.
dek: Lots of families straddle the Hudson. When a parent moves from Bergen County to Rockland, or from Queens to Hackensack, some things move with them and some have to start over. Here is the list.
keyFacts: Medicaid is state by state: apply in the new state after the move
Medicare plan switch window: the month you move plus 2 full months after
New York license exchange: within 30 days of becoming a resident
New Jersey license, title and registration transfer: within 60 days
NY estate tax exclusion for 2026 deaths: $7,350,000; NJ has no estate tax, only inheritance tax
body:
When a parent moves between New Jersey and New York, Medicare follows them but Medicaid does not. Medicaid is run by each state, so your parent has to apply in the new state. Property tax relief, the driver's license and voter registration also have to be redone, each on its own deadline.

The two states sit side by side, and plenty of families have a parent in one and kids in the other. A move to be closer makes sense. This guide covers what to do in each direction, using each state's own rules.

For the New Jersey side of anything here, our sister site Seniors of NJ covers the Garden State's programs in depth.

What happens to Medicaid when a parent moves?

It ends in the old state and has to be applied for again in the new one. The federal Medicaid agency says people generally must be residents of the state where they get Medicaid. Coverage generally stops at the end of the month a person no longer meets a state's rules.

The good news is that the new state can't make your parent wait. Under federal rules, a state may not deny Medicaid because someone hasn't lived there for a set period. Once your mom or dad lives in the new state and intends to stay, they can apply.

  1. Apply in the new state right after the move. In New York, apply through the local Department of Social Services (HRA in the five boroughs) or call the New York Medicaid Helpline at 800-541-2831. In New Jersey, apply through the state's Medicaid program.
  2. Ask about retroactive coverage. Federal rules let Medicaid cover bills for up to three months before the month of application if your parent would have qualified then.
  3. Close the old case. Tell the old state's Medicaid office the moving date so coverage ends cleanly.
  4. Line up care before the move. Home care hours, a nursing home bed or a managed long-term care plan in one state doesn't carry over. Each has to be set up again under the new state's program.

The rules differ between the states, so a parent who qualified in one may not in the other. For nursing home care, New York looks back 60 months (five years) at gifts and transfers of assets, so ask the new state about its rules before moving money. Our New York Medicaid guide covers the New York limits and how to apply.

Plan the Medicaid application before the moving truck. A gap in coverage is hardest on a parent who needs daily care.

What about Medicare and Medicare Advantage?

Original Medicare (Parts A and B) is a federal program, so it keeps working in both states. Just update the address with Social Security. Medicare Advantage and Part D drug plans are different, because they serve set areas.

Medicare gives a Special Enrollment Period for a move. If your parent moves out of the plan's service area, or stays in it but has new plan options, they can switch to a new Medicare Advantage or Part D plan.

SituationWindow to switch plans
Told the plan before movingStarts the month before the move, lasts 2 full months after
Told the plan after movingStarts the month of the move, lasts 2 full months after
Moved out of a Medicare Advantage area and picked nothingEnrolled in Original Medicare when the old plan drops them
Has Medicaid or Extra HelpCan change drug coverage once a calendar month

A parent dropped back into Original Medicare should check that they still have drug coverage. Call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) for help comparing plans in the new ZIP code. See our Medicare enrollment guide for how to compare plans.

How does property tax relief change?

Both states help older homeowners with property taxes, but the programs are completely different, and none of them follows your parent across the border. A move resets the clock.

Moving into New York

  • STAR credit. New homeowners register for the STAR credit, a check from the Tax Department for school taxes. The older STAR exemption on the tax bill isn't open to new homeowners. To get the credit for a year, your parent must own and live in the home as of July 1.
  • Enhanced STAR. At least one resident owner must be 65 by December 31 of the benefit year. The income limit is $110,750 or less for 2026 benefits and $113,550 or less for 2027 benefits.
  • Senior citizens exemption. Outside New York City, localities can cut the taxable assessment by up to 50% for owners 65 and older. Each locality sets its income limit between $3,000 and $50,000. Your parent generally must own the home for 12 straight months before filing, unless they had the exemption on a prior New York home. In New York City the Department of Finance runs its own version.

Our guides to STAR and Enhanced STAR and the senior homeowners exemption walk through each one.

Moving into New Jersey

New Jersey runs ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ side by side and sends each applicant one benefit statement showing all three. All three look back at where and how your parent lived in earlier years.

  • Stay NJ. For the 2025 tax year, the homeowner (or spouse) must have been 65 or older during 2025, and owned and lived in the home for all 12 months of 2025. The New Jersey Division of Taxation says the 2027 budget provides Stay NJ payments for applicants with incomes of $200,000 or less, and lists a maximum benefit of $6,500 for income up to $100,000.
  • Senior Freeze. It repays increases in property tax on a main home. You have to meet every rule for each year from the base year through the application year, so a newcomer has to build that history first.
  • ANCHOR. It is for New Jersey residents who own or rent their main home in the state, with this year's benefit based on residency, income and age in 2025.

The deadline for the 2025 New Jersey application was November 2, 2026. A parent who moves to New Jersey this winter would look at later application years.

Which state taxes your parent's income?

Generally the state where your parent is domiciled. The New York Tax Department defines domicile as the permanent home you intend to return to. You can have several residences but only one domicile.

Leaving New York takes more than a new address. New York says your domicile doesn't change until you show with clear and convincing evidence that you've left and set up a new home elsewhere. Registering to vote in the new state isn't enough by itself. The department looks at every part of a person's life.

New York can also tax someone as a resident who isn't domiciled there. That happens when a person keeps a permanent place to live in the state for substantially all of the year and spends 184 days or more in New York. Any part of a day counts.

  • The year of the move. A part-year resident files New York's Form IT-203, with income split between resident and nonresident periods.
  • Keeping the old house. If your parent moves to New Jersey but keeps the house in Nassau County and spends lots of time there, the 184-day rule matters. Keep a calendar.
  • New York City and Yonkers. New York City has its own resident income tax, and Yonkers adds a resident surcharge on the state return.

New Jersey has its own rules for who counts as a resident. Check with the New Jersey Division of Taxation or a tax preparer licensed in both states. Our New York retirement income tax guide covers how New York taxes pensions and Social Security.

When does the license, car and voter registration have to move?

The deadlines are short, and they differ by direction.

TaskMoving into New YorkMoving into New Jersey
Driver's licenseExchange within 30 days of becoming a resident, in person at a DMV officeTransfer within 60 days of the move or before the old license expires, whichever comes first
Vehicle title and registrationRegister with the NY DMVTransfer within 60 days of the move
Voter registrationRegister online with a NY.gov ID, by mail or at the DMVRegister with New Jersey election officials

For a New York license exchange, the old license must have a photo, be valid or expired less than 24 months, and have been issued at least 6 months before. Your parent will need a vision test at the DMV or a completed MV-619 eye test report. New York treats living in the state for 90 days as presumed residency.

If your parent no longer drives, both states issue non-driver ID cards. Our older drivers guide has more on driving in New York.

When leaving New York, cancel the old registration. The New York State Board of Elections says this takes a written letter to the county board of elections. Email won't do.

How do estate tax and inheritance tax differ?

This is one of the biggest differences, and it depends on where your parent lives when they die. New York's tax is an estate tax, based on the size of the whole estate. New Jersey has no estate tax for deaths on or after January 1, 2018, but it still has an inheritance tax based on who inherits.

TopicNew YorkNew Jersey
Estate taxYes. 2026 basic exclusion: $7,350,000None for deaths on or after Jan. 1, 2018
What decides the taxThe size of the whole estateWho inherits and how much each gets
Spouse, children, grandchildren, parents, stepchildrenSee the estate tax rulesClass A, exempt from inheritance tax
Brothers, sisters, sons- and daughters-in-lawSee the estate tax rulesClass C: first $25,000 free, then 11% to 16%
DeadlineForm ET-706 within nine months of deathReturn and tax within eight months of death

Real estate can pull the other state in. A New Jersey resident who owns a New York house may owe New York estate tax as a nonresident if the estate is over the exclusion. A New York resident with a New Jersey house may face New Jersey nonresident inheritance tax on it if it passes to someone outside Class A. See our New York estate tax guide and probate guide.

Before the move

Get the Medicaid application ready for the new state. Note the Medicare plan window. Check which property tax programs your parent will lose and when new ones can start. Put the 30-day or 60-day license deadline on the calendar. Have the will reviewed by a lawyer in the new state.

A move is also a good time to look again at your parent's health care proxy and power of attorney, so the papers fit the state where they will be used.

faq.q: My mom has Medicaid in Bergen County. If she moves in with me in Rockland County, does it transfer?
faq.a: No. Medicaid is run by each state, so she has to apply in New York once she lives here. New York can't make her wait a set period first. Apply through the Rockland County Department of Social Services, and tell New Jersey the moving date so her case closes.

faq.q: We're moving Dad from Staten Island to New Jersey. How long does he have to get a NJ license?
faq.a: New Jersey's Motor Vehicle Commission says he must transfer his out-of-state license within 60 days of the move or before the current license expires, whichever comes first. The car's title and registration also have to move within 60 days.

faq.q: Can my parent keep a Medicare Advantage plan after moving from New Jersey to New York?
faq.a: Only if the plan serves the new address. If not, Medicare gives a Special Enrollment Period to switch. It runs from the month of the move (or the month before, if the plan was told first) through 2 full months after.

faq.q: How soon must a new New York resident get a New York license?
faq.a: Within 30 days of becoming a resident, in person at a DMV office. New York treats living in the state for 90 days as presumed residency.

faq.q: Does New Jersey have an estate tax?
faq.a: Not for deaths on or after January 1, 2018. New Jersey still has an inheritance tax, but spouses, children, grandchildren, parents and stepchildren are Class A beneficiaries and exempt. New York has an estate tax with a 2026 exclusion of $7,350,000.

faq.q: Does Enhanced STAR follow a parent who moves to New York?
faq.a: No. STAR belongs to the home. A new homeowner registers for the STAR credit. For Enhanced STAR, one resident owner must be 65 by December 31 of the benefit year, with income of $113,550 or less for 2027 benefits.

title: Moving a parent between New York and Pennsylvania: what changes
seoTitle: Moving a Parent From NY to PA: What Changes
seoDesc: Moving a parent from New York to Pennsylvania? Compare EPIC and PACE, STAR and the PA rent rebate, taxes, Medicaid, Medicare and license deadlines side by side.
dek: Medicare moves with your parent. EPIC, STAR, Medicaid and the driver's license do not. Here is how New York and Pennsylvania compare, with each state's own figures and the aging office for each NJ-near PA county.
keyFacts: PACE and PACENET need 90 days of Pennsylvania residency
EPIC needs a permanent home in New York
PA Property Tax/Rent Rebate: income $48,110 or less, up to $1,000
Medicare moving window: the move month plus two full months
New license: 60 days in PA, 30 days in NY
body:
When a parent moves between New York and Pennsylvania, Medicare comes along but almost everything state-run starts over. EPIC, STAR, New York Medicaid and the New York driver's license stay behind, and your parent applies for Pennsylvania's own programs (or the other way around) once the new home is their permanent address.

Most families moving a parent from New York toward New Jersey's western edge look at Pike, Monroe, Wayne, Bucks or Northampton County. This guide compares the programs that change, using each state's own figures, and gives the aging office for each of those counties. It does not say one state is better. The right answer depends on your parent's income, home and health.

What happens to my parent's prescription coverage?

Medicare Part D is federal, so a Part D plan can continue if it serves the new area. The state program on top of it changes. New York's EPIC requires a permanent home in New York. Pennsylvania's PACE and PACENET require being a Pennsylvania resident for at least 90 days before applying.

EPIC (New York)PACE (Pennsylvania)PACENET (Pennsylvania)
Age65 or older65 or older65 or older
ResidencyPermanent home in New York (not a summer or winter home)Pennsylvania resident at least 90 days before applyingSame as PACE
Income limitBelow $75,000 single, $100,000 married$14,500 or less single, $17,700 or less married$14,501 to $33,500 single, $17,701 to $41,500 married
Income yearPrevious calendar yearPrevious calendar yearPrevious calendar year
What you pay$3 to $20 per prescription after Part D$6 generic, $9 brand (2025 PACE manual)$8 generic, $15 brand, after a monthly deductible (2025 PACE manual)
Phone1-800-332-37421-800-225-72231-800-225-7223

The PACE and PACENET copays are as listed in the PA Department of Aging's 2025 PACE manual. It says PACENET members meet a monthly deductible set from the Medicare Part D benchmark premium. Pennsylvania says PACE works with Part D, Medicare Advantage, retiree and employer plans and VA benefits. If your parent cannot get PACE or PACENET, the PACE Clearinghouse may help with drug costs. Apply by phone at 1-800-225-7223, online, or by mail.

Do not mix up the names. Pennsylvania's PACE is a prescription program. The Medicare and Medicaid PACE care program is something else, covered in our PACE guide.

The 90-day rule matters for timing. A parent moving to Milford or Stroudsburg will rely on Part D (or other drug coverage) alone for at least the first 90 days. Plan for that if they take costly brand-name drugs. Moving the other way, EPIC's eligibility page lists no waiting period, only a permanent home in New York. See our EPIC guide.

How do property tax breaks compare?

New York lowers the tax bill up front. Pennsylvania pays a rebate on property taxes or rent. Neither moves with your parent.

ProgramWho qualifiesIncome limitBenefit
Enhanced STAR (NY)A resident owner 65 or older by December 31 of the benefit year$110,750 or less for 2026 benefits, $113,550 or less for 2027Lower school property taxes
Senior citizens exemption (NY)Owners generally 65 or older, where the locality offers itSet locally, between $3,000 and $50,000, with smaller exemptions up to $58,400 where adoptedUp to 50% off the taxable assessment
Property Tax/Rent Rebate (PA)65 or older, widows and widowers 50 or older, or people with disabilities 18 or older; homeowners and rentersHousehold income of $48,110 or lessStandard rebate up to $1,000; a supplemental $190 to $500 for some homeowners with income of $32,070 or less whose property taxes are over 15% of income

In New York, register for the STAR credit with the Tax Department as soon as a home becomes the primary residence. Outside New York City, file the senior exemption on Form RP-467 with the local assessor, by March 1 in most places. In Pennsylvania, apply at mypath.pa.gov, by mail or in person, or call 1-888-222-9190. The current rebate deadline is December 31, 2026, and applications postmarked by that date are accepted. Pennsylvania's rebate also covers renters. Our STAR guide and senior exemption guide cover the New York forms.

How are retirement income and inheritances taxed?

Income tax

Both states go easy on retirement income, in different ways. Pennsylvania's personal income tax guide lists Social Security and distributions from eligible Pennsylvania retirement plans after retirement age as never taxable compensation. It also says an early withdrawal from a regular or Roth IRA is taxable to the extent it exceeds contributions already taxed. Pennsylvania notes that a plan being qualified for federal tax does not decide its state treatment.

New York lets you subtract Social Security included in federal income. People 59½ or older can exclude up to $20,000 of qualified pension and annuity income. New York State, local government and federal government pensions can be subtracted at any age. Our New York retirement income guide has the details.

Inheritance tax and estate tax

Pennsylvania taxes what heirs receive. New York taxes large estates.

  • Pennsylvania inheritance tax. 0% to a surviving spouse or to a parent from a child 21 or younger, 4.5% to direct descendants and lineal heirs, 12% to siblings and 15% to other heirs. Charities, exempt institutions and tax-exempt government entities are left out of the 15% group. The tax is due at death and becomes delinquent nine months after. Paying within three months earns a 5% discount.
  • New York estate tax. For deaths in 2026, the basic exclusion amount is $7,350,000. A resident's estate files a New York return if the federal gross estate plus includible gifts is over that amount. A nonresident's estate may also have to file if it includes real or tangible property in New York and is over the same amount.

That last point catches families who move a parent to Pennsylvania but keep the house in Rockland or Westchester. Talk with an estate attorney before the move. See our New York estate tax guide and probate guide.

Medicare moves with your parent. Medicaid, EPIC, STAR and the license do not.

What happens to Medicare and Medicaid?

Medicare

Original Medicare lets your parent use any doctor or hospital that takes Medicare, so it works after the move. Medicare Advantage and Part D plans have service areas. When your parent moves out of the plan's area, Medicare gives a Special Enrollment Period to switch to a new Medicare Advantage or drug plan, or go back to Original Medicare. It begins the month of the move and lasts two full months after. If they tell the plan before moving, it starts the month before. Moving into or out of a nursing home or rehab hospital opens its own window too. Fall open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7; see our open enrollment guide.

Medicaid

Medicaid does not transfer. Each state runs its own program, so your parent applies again in the new state. Pennsylvania says Medicaid is available to Pennsylvania residents regardless of how long they have lived there. Adults 65 and older and people getting long-term care are judged under non-MAGI rules, and long-term services for older adults run through Community HealthChoices.

Apply in Pennsylvania through COMPASS at compass.dhs.pa.gov, by phone at 1-866-550-4355, at the County Assistance Office or by mail. Tell New York's local Department of Social Services (or HRA in New York City) about the move so the case closes cleanly. Our New York Medicaid guide covers the New York side.

How soon does my parent need a new driver's license?

  • Moving to Pennsylvania. PennDOT says new residents with an out-of-state license must get a Pennsylvania license within 60 days. Fill out Form DL-180R, bring proof of identity and residency and a Social Security card, pass a vision test and surrender the New York license. It must be valid or expired no more than six months.
  • Moving to New York. New York DMV says new residents must exchange an out-of-state license within 30 days. It is done in person at a DMV office. Bring Form MV-44 and the old license, and pass a vision test at DMV or bring an Eye Test Report (MV-619).

If your parent no longer drives, they can get a non-driver ID instead. Our older drivers guide covers that decision.

Who do I call in the Pennsylvania county my parent is moving to?

In Pennsylvania, local help for older adults runs through county Area Agencies on Aging. Call the one for the new address and ask about meals, care assessments, Medicare counseling (PA MEDI) and help with the rent rebate.

CountyOffice and addressPhone
PikePike County Area Agency on Aging, 150 Pike County Blvd., Lords Valley, PA 18428570-775-5550, toll free 800-233-8911
MonroeMonroe County Area Agency on Aging, 724 Phillips Street, Suite 102, Stroudsburg, PA 18360570-420-3735, toll free 1-800-498-0330
WayneWayne County Area Agency on Aging, 323 Tenth Street, Honesdale, PA 18431570-253-4262
BucksBucks County Area Agency on Aging, 55 E Court Street, 3rd Floor, Doylestown, PA 18901267-880-5700
NorthamptonNorthampton County Area Agency on Aging (call for the office address)610-829-4540

Pennsylvania's statewide 24-hour line for reporting abuse of an older adult is 1-800-490-8505, and reports can be anonymous. If your parent is moving the other way, into New York, start with the county Office for the Aging; see our NY Connects guide.

What order should we do things in?

  1. Price the drugs first. Look up your parent's medicines on Part D plans in the new ZIP code. Remember PACE and PACENET start only after 90 days of Pennsylvania residency.
  2. Call the new county's aging office. Ask about meals, assessments and PA MEDI counseling before the move date.
  3. Tell the Medicare plan the moving date. Telling it before the move opens the Special Enrollment Period a month early.
  4. Apply for Medicaid in the new state if needed. Use COMPASS in Pennsylvania. Close the New York case with the local Department of Social Services or HRA.
  5. Change the license. 60 days in Pennsylvania, 30 days in New York.
  6. Sort out the old home. Ask the New York assessor what happens to STAR and senior exemptions once the home is no longer the primary residence, and ask an attorney about New York estate tax if your parent keeps New York property.
  7. Apply for the new state's tax relief. Pennsylvania's Property Tax/Rent Rebate deadline for the current year is December 31, 2026. In New York, register for STAR once the home is the primary residence.

For a parent with a home on each side of the river near Port Jervis, see our tri-state guide.

faq.q: My mom is moving from Rockland County to Milford, PA. When does she lose EPIC and get PACE?
faq.a: EPIC is for people whose permanent home is in New York, so it ends once Milford becomes her permanent home. PACE and PACENET need 90 days of Pennsylvania residency before she applies. Keep her Part D plan, or switch it during the moving Special Enrollment Period if it does not serve Pike County. Call PACE at 1-800-225-7223.

faq.q: My dad in Staten Island is moving near us in Bucks County. Can he keep his Medicare Advantage plan?
faq.a: Only if the plan serves Bucks County. If it does not, Medicare gives him a Special Enrollment Period that starts the month he moves (or the month before, if he tells the plan first) and lasts two full months after. The Bucks County Area Agency on Aging, 267-880-5700, offers free Medicare counseling through PA MEDI.

faq.q: Does Pennsylvania tax my parent's pension and Social Security?
faq.a: Pennsylvania's tax guide lists Social Security and distributions from eligible Pennsylvania retirement plans after retirement age as never taxable. Early IRA withdrawals can be taxable. Check how the specific plan is treated, since federal qualified status does not decide it.

faq.q: Will my parent's New York Medicaid home care continue after a move to Pennsylvania?
faq.a: No. Medicaid does not transfer between states. Your parent applies in Pennsylvania through COMPASS, by phone at 1-866-550-4355 or at the County Assistance Office. Pennsylvania has no minimum time as a resident for Medicaid.

faq.q: If Dad moves to Pennsylvania but keeps his house in Westchester, does New York estate tax still matter?
faq.a: It can. Tax.ny.gov says a nonresident's estate may have to file a New York estate tax return if it includes real or tangible property in New York and is over the basic exclusion amount, which is $7,350,000 for 2026 deaths. Pennsylvania inheritance tax may also apply. Ask an estate attorney.

faq.q: How soon does my mother need a Pennsylvania driver's license?
faq.a: PennDOT says within 60 days of becoming a resident. She fills out Form DL-180R, brings proof of identity and residency and her Social Security card, passes a vision test and surrenders her New York license.
