title: Probate in New York: Surrogate's Court steps, fees and timing
seoTitle: Probate in New York: Steps, Fees and Small Estates
seoDesc: How probate works in New York's Surrogate's Court: when a will must be probated, the $50,000 small estate route, administration without a will, fees and timing.
dek: When a parent dies in New York, their property usually passes through the Surrogate's Court. Here is which proceeding you need, what to file, what the court charges and how long creditors have.
keyFacts: Estates are handled by the Surrogate's Court in the county of primary residence
Small estate route: personal property of $50,000 or less
Small estate filing fee: $1
Probate and administration fees run from $45 to $1,250 by estate value
Creditors generally have 7 months from when letters are first issued
body:
Probate in New York is the Surrogate's Court process that confirms a will is valid and appoints the executor to settle the estate. If there's no will, the court runs an administration proceeding instead, and if the person left $50,000 or less in personal property, a simpler small estate process may apply.

Every county in New York has a Surrogate's Court, including each of the five boroughs. You file in the county where the person who died had their primary residence. This guide walks through which proceeding fits, the steps, the court fees and how long it tends to take.

Which proceeding do you need?

The court uses a few terms you'll hear often. The person who died is the decedent. Their property is the estate. The close relatives who would inherit under state law are the distributees. The person named in the will to settle the estate is the executor.

SituationProceeding
Left a will, more than $50,000 in personal property, or real estate in their name aloneProbate
No will, more than $50,000 in personal property, or real estate in their name aloneAdministration
Personal property of $50,000 or less, with or without a willSmall estate (voluntary administration)
A wrongful death or other lawsuit may followProbate or administration, even if the estate is small

Personal property means things other than real estate, such as cash, bank accounts, stocks, bonds, cars and artwork. Real property means houses and land.

What usually passes outside probate?

Some assets go straight to a named person and never enter the estate. Common examples are accounts with a named beneficiary, such as life insurance, retirement accounts and payable-on-death bank accounts, plus property held jointly with a right of survivorship. Check each account's paperwork. These assets often make an estate small enough for the simpler process, or leave nothing to probate at all.

When does a will have to be probated?

If your parent left a will and owned property that passes under it, the original will must be filed with the Surrogate's Court and admitted to probate. Until the court admits the will and appoints the executor, nobody has legal authority to collect and distribute those assets.

Whoever holds the original will should keep it safe and unaltered. The court needs the original itself.

  1. Gather documents. Get the original will and a certified death certificate. Make a list of assets and debts.
  2. Identify everyone with a stake. List all distributees and every beneficiary named in the will, with addresses.
  3. File the probate petition. File it with the original will, the death certificate and supporting papers in the Surrogate's Court of your parent's county. Some counties accept filing online through NYSCEF, the state's electronic filing system.
  4. Get waivers or serve citations. Each distributee must be served with a notice called a citation, or sign a waiver and consent to the executor's appointment.
  5. Notify beneficiaries. Beneficiaries who inherit under the will must be officially told about the proceeding.
  6. The court admits the will. Once the Surrogate is satisfied the will is valid, the executor is appointed and can begin settling the estate.

A distributee who disagrees can appear in court and object. Objections slow everything down, so it helps to talk with family early about what the will says.

What is the small estate route?

New York's small estate process is called voluntary administration. It applies when the decedent's personal property has a gross value of $50,000 or less, with or without a will. Certain property set aside for the surviving family under state law isn't counted toward that limit.

What should you bring?

  • A certified copy of the death certificate.
  • The original will, if there is one.
  • A list of personal property with rough values: bank accounts, stocks, bonds, cars.
  • Names and addresses of the closest relatives.

Real estate changes the picture. If your parent owned a house or land in their name alone, the estate isn't small, and you need probate or administration. If the real estate was owned jointly with someone else, it can still be a small estate.

The court appoints a voluntary administrator. That's the executor if there's a will, or the closest distributee if there isn't. You file a small estate affidavit petition with a certified death certificate, plus the original will if there is one. The filing fee is $1. The courts' free Small Estate DIY program builds the forms for you, step by step.

Start with a list of every account and who it names. That one list tells you which court process you need.

What happens when there's no will?

If your parent died without a will, an administration proceeding lets the court appoint an administrator. Usually the closest family member files. The court then issues letters of administration, which give that person authority to collect and distribute the property according to law.

To start, gather a copy of the paid funeral bill and a certified death certificate. List your parent's debts and assets. Then file a petition for letters of administration in the Surrogate's Court, naming every distributee. Each distributee is served with a citation, or signs a waiver and consent.

Real estate works differently when there's no will. Under New York law, real property passes to the distributees at death. Depending on who survives, a court proceeding may not be needed just for the house. The courts suggest talking with a real estate attorney and the local tax office about how to handle the title.

In New York City, each borough is its own county with its own Surrogate's Court. So a parent who lived in Flushing files in Queens County Surrogate's Court, and one who lived in Park Slope files in Kings County (Brooklyn). The courts' online Court Locator lists addresses for every county.

Who inherits without a will?

New York's intestacy law, Estates, Powers and Trusts Law section 4-1.1, sets the order.

  • Spouse and children. The spouse gets $50,000 plus half of the rest. The children share the remainder.
  • Spouse, no children. The spouse gets everything.
  • Children, no spouse. The children share everything. A child who died earlier is represented by their own children.
  • No spouse or children. Surviving parents inherit. If none, brothers and sisters and their descendants inherit.

What does probate cost in New York?

The court's filing fee for probate or administration depends on the value of the estate. The schedule is set in section 2402 of the Surrogate's Court Procedure Act.

Estate valueFiling fee
Under $10,000$45
$10,000 to under $20,000$75
$20,000 to under $50,000$215
$50,000 to under $100,000$280
$100,000 to under $250,000$420
$250,000 to under $500,000$625
$500,000 and over$1,250
Small estate (voluntary administration)$1

Other costs can include certified copies, a bond if the will or the court requires one, and lawyers' fees. Many people handle simple estates on their own, and the courts offer DIY forms and a free Ask a Law Librarian service. A lawyer is worth considering when the will is unclear, a family member objects, there's a business or out-of-state property, or the estate may owe New York estate tax.

How long does probate take?

No official timeline applies to every estate. A simple, uncontested case where every distributee signs a waiver moves faster than one where citations must be served or someone objects.

One date matters for nearly every estate. Under Surrogate's Court Procedure Act section 1802, creditors generally have 7 months from the date letters are first issued to present claims. An executor who pays debts and distributions in good faith before a late claim arrives isn't personally liable for those payments. Even so, many executors wait out the 7 months before making final distributions so that bills can be paid first.

After that, the executor or administrator collects assets, pays valid debts and taxes, sells or transfers property, and distributes what's left. Keep a clear record of every dollar in and out.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Spending estate money before appointment. Until letters are issued, nobody has authority over estate accounts. A power of attorney ends at death and can't be used.
  • Mixing money. Open a separate estate account once appointed. Don't run estate money through your own account.
  • Forgetting the house. A house in your parent's name alone needs probate or administration even if the bank accounts are small.
  • Losing the original will. A copy usually isn't enough. Keep the original safe from the start.
  • Paying heirs first. Pay valid debts and taxes before distributions, and keep receipts.

If the estate is large, read our guide to New York estate tax early, since that return is due nine months after death. The power of attorney guide explains why those papers stop working at death.

faq.q: Do I have to probate my mom's will in Queens if she only had a bank account?
faq.a: It depends on the account. If the account named a beneficiary or was joint with survivorship, it may pass outside probate. If it was in her name alone and worth $50,000 or less, and she owned no real estate in her name alone, you can likely use the small estate process in Queens County Surrogate's Court for a $1 filing fee.

faq.q: How do I handle my dad's estate in Albany if he had no will?
faq.a: File a petition for letters of administration in the Albany County Surrogate's Court, naming all distributees and attaching a certified death certificate and a copy of the paid funeral bill. If his personal property was $50,000 or less and he owned no real estate in his name alone, the small estate process may apply instead.

faq.q: What is the small estate limit in New York?
faq.a: Personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting certain property set aside for the family under state law. Real estate in the decedent's name alone takes the estate out of the small estate process.

faq.q: How much does probate cost in New York?
faq.a: The court's filing fee ranges from $45 for estates under $10,000 to $1,250 for estates of $500,000 or more. A small estate costs $1 to file. Lawyer fees, bonds and certified copies are extra.

faq.q: How long do creditors have to file claims against a New York estate?
faq.a: Generally 7 months from the date letters are first issued to an executor or administrator. A fiduciary who pays lawful claims and distributions in good faith before a late claim arrives is not personally liable for those payments.

faq.q: Can I file probate papers online in New York?
faq.a: In some counties, yes, through NYSCEF, the New York State Courts Electronic Filing system. Check the courts' e-filing county list or call your county's Surrogate's Court.

title: MTA reduced fare for 65+: half-price subway, bus and train rides
seoTitle: MTA Reduced Fare for Seniors 65+: How to Apply
seoDesc: New Yorkers 65 and older pay $1.50 on MTA subways and buses with a Reduced-Fare OMNY card. How to apply, LIRR and Metro-North discounts, upstate senior fares.
dek: At 65, New Yorkers can ride MTA subways and local buses for half price and get up to half off on the commuter railroads. Here is how to get the Reduced-Fare OMNY card, and what other New York transit systems offer.
keyFacts: Riders 65+ pay $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare
Express bus: $3.60, except weekday peak hours
LIRR and Metro-North: up to 50% off the one-way peak fare
After 12 paid rides in seven days with OMNY, the rest of the week is free
OMNY customer service: 877-789-6669, 24/7
body:
New Yorkers 65 and older qualify for MTA reduced fare, which cuts the subway and local bus fare to $1.50, half the $3 base fare. You apply once for a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, in person or by mail, and riders 65 and up can often get the card the same day at an MTA Customer Service Center.

The discount also applies on the Staten Island Railway, Select Bus Service and express buses outside rush hour, and up to half off on the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) and Metro-North. This guide covers how to apply, what to bring, how the discount works on each service, and senior fares on other New York transit systems.

Who qualifies for MTA reduced fare?

Anyone 65 or older qualifies on age alone. No income test applies.

People under 65 can qualify with a disability. That includes people receiving Medicare benefits for a reason other than age, and people with serious mental illness who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI). They use a separate disability application.

What if your parent is under 65?

A spouse or parent under 65 may still qualify through the disability route. Someone who gets Medicare because of a disability, rather than age, meets the test. So does someone with serious mental illness who receives SSI. Other qualifying disabilities are listed on the MTA's disability application.

The disability application is a separate form. By mail, include the same photo and ID as the age application, plus documentation of the disability. In person, Customer Service Center staff can help, though disability applications are more likely to need further review than a simple age application.

Reduced fare is different from Access-A-Ride. Access-A-Ride is door-to-door paratransit for people whose disability keeps them off buses and subways. If that fits your parent, see our Access-A-Ride guide.

How much do you save?

ServiceFull fareReduced fare
Subway, Staten Island Railway$3$1.50, at all times
Local, limited and Select Bus Service$3$1.50, at all times
Express bus$7.25$3.60, except weekdays 6 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m.
LIRR and Metro-NorthVaries by tripUp to 50% off the one-way peak fare, with morning peak limits

OMNY also caps what you pay. With a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, once you've paid for 12 rides in seven days, the rest of your rides that week are free. Free transfers between buses and subways still work, as they did with MetroCard.

For a parent who rides every day, the weekly cap means a busy week of errands costs no more than 12 half-price rides.

How do you apply?

The online application is not available right now. You can apply in person or by mail.

In person (fastest)

Visit an MTA Customer Service Center at select accessible subway stations, the office at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan (weekdays), or an MTA Mobile Sales van. Applicants 65 and older can often walk out with the card the same day, though some applications need more review.

By mail

  1. Get the age application. There are separate forms for age and for disability. Use the one for riders 65 and older.
  2. Add a photo. Include a passport-style photo, 2 by 1.5 inches.
  3. Copy your ID. Include a copy of a valid ID that shows your date of birth (see the list below).
  4. Mail it. Send everything to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625.
  5. Allow time. The MTA says new mail applicants may wait up to three months for the card.
  6. Set up the card. When it arrives, load money on it online with a free OMNY account.

What ID is accepted?

  • A valid driver's license from any state
  • A valid passport from any country
  • An IDNYC card
  • A valid state photo ID
  • A birth certificate or Medicare card, each paired with a photo ID

A Medicare card on its own isn't enough for the application. Pair it with a photo ID.

Helping a parent who doesn't use the internet

Go with them to a Customer Service Center. You'll skip the mail wait, and they can often leave with a working card. Ask the agent to show you both how to tap and how to add money.

What does that look like in a real week?

Say your mom takes the bus to the senior center and back three days a week, plus four other trips for shopping and appointments. That's 10 rides. At full fare she'd pay $30. With reduced fare she pays $15. Because of the 12-ride weekly cap, the most she can pay for subway and local bus rides in any seven days is $18, no matter how often she rides.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Waiting for the online form. It isn't available right now. Apply in person or by mail.
  • Sending a Medicare card alone. It counts as ID only with a photo ID.
  • Using the wrong form. There are separate applications for age and disability. Riders 65 and older use the age form.
  • Taking an express bus at rush hour. The $3.60 reduced express fare doesn't apply weekdays from 6 to 10 a.m. and 3 to 7 p.m.
  • Buying a multi-trip rail ticket. Reduced fare on the LIRR and Metro-North is sold as one-way tickets only.

How does the discount work on the LIRR and Metro-North?

Riders 65 and older pay half of the one-way peak fare on the LIRR and Metro-North. There are morning rush limits.

  • LIRR. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Avenue or Long Island City between 6 and 10 a.m.
  • Metro-North. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 a.m.
  • Evening peak trains are fine on both railroads.
  • Multi-trip tickets have no reduced-fare version.

If your parent has a morning appointment in Manhattan, plan a train that arrives before 6 a.m. or after 10 a.m., or pay the regular fare for that one ride. The trip home in the afternoon or evening can use a reduced-fare ticket, even at rush hour.

Reduced-fare tickets are sold at ticket offices and on the train. Be ready to show one form of ID. The railroads accept a Reduced-Fare OMNY card or MetroCard (it doesn't need money on it), a paratransit card such as Access-A-Ride, Able-Ride or SCAT, a Medicare card, or a driver's license, birth certificate or passport showing you're over 65. A Medicaid card is not accepted.

What do other New York transit systems charge seniors?

Outside the MTA area, each region runs its own buses. Federal rules say transit systems that get federal money can charge seniors, people with disabilities and Medicare cardholders no more than half the peak fare during off-peak hours on fixed routes. Here's what three of the larger systems say.

SystemAreaSenior rule
NFTA-MetroBuffalo and Niagara FallsHalf fare for riders 65 and older, all day, with an NFTA reduced-fare card ($2). Call 716-855-6611.
CDTACapital RegionHalf-fare passes and reduced cash fares for riders 65 and older. A Medicare card can be used instead of a CDTA reduced-fare card on regularly scheduled buses. Call 518-482-8822.
CentroSyracuse and Central New YorkHalf fare for riders 65 and older with a Centro reduced-fare photo ID, or a Medicare card plus photo ID. Call 315-442-3400.

For NFTA, download the Reduced Fare Application from the NFTA website. Photos are taken at the Metropolitan Transportation Center, 181 Ellicott Street in Buffalo, weekdays 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., or at the Portage Road Transportation Center in Niagara Falls by appointment. For Centro, visit a Centro office with a photo ID and proof of birth date. The processing fee is $2, cash only.

For CDTA, reduced-fare ID cards are issued by the county Departments for the Aging in Albany, Schenectady and Saratoga counties, with a one-time $3 fee.

For other counties, call your county's transit system or Office for the Aging. NY Connects can help you find them at 1-800-342-9871.

Where can you get help with your card?

For OMNY card problems, call OMNY customer service at 877-789-6669, 24 hours a day. For Reduced-Fare MetroCard questions, call 511 and say "MTA," then "Subway and Buses." Relay users can call 711.

Transit savings add up, but they're one piece of a budget. If your parent is on a fixed income, our guide to free and discounted programs in New York lists other ways to save, and the Medicare Savings Program guide may help with health costs.

faq.q: How do I get my dad a senior MetroCard in Manhattan?
faq.a: The MTA now issues a Reduced-Fare OMNY card instead. Take him to an MTA Customer Service Center or the office at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan with a valid photo ID. Riders 65 and older can often get the card the same day.

faq.q: How much is the subway for seniors in NYC?
faq.a: Riders 65 and older pay $1.50 on subways and local buses, half the $3 base fare. After 12 paid rides in seven days on a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, the rest of that week's rides are free.

faq.q: Can my mom in Westchester use her Medicare card for a discount on Metro-North?
faq.a: Yes. A Medicare card is one of the IDs Metro-North accepts for a reduced-fare ticket, which is half the one-way peak fare. Reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 a.m.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a Reduced-Fare OMNY card by mail?
faq.a: The MTA says new mail applicants may wait up to three months. Applying in person is faster, and riders 65 and older can often get the card the same day.

faq.q: Can I apply for MTA reduced fare online?
faq.a: Not right now. The MTA says the online application is not available. Apply in person at a Customer Service Center or Mobile Sales van, or by mail to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625.

faq.q: Do seniors get a discount on LIRR?
faq.a: Yes. Riders 65 and older pay half the one-way peak fare. The discount isn't valid on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Avenue or Long Island City between 6 and 10 a.m.

title: Scams aimed at older New Yorkers and where to report them
seoTitle: Scams Targeting Older New Yorkers and Where to Report
seoDesc: Grandparent, Medicare, Social Security, utility, tech support and romance scams in New York, and who to call: the Attorney General, DFS, FTC, police and APS.
dek: Most scams aimed at older adults follow the same script: a familiar name, an emergency, a rush and a strange way to pay. Here is how the common ones work in New York and exactly who to call.
keyFacts: NY Attorney General scam complaints: 1-800-771-7755
NYS Department of Financial Services: 1-800-342-3736
Medicare fraud: 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227)
Social Security scams: report at oig.ssa.gov
Statewide Adult Protective Services helpline: 1-844-697-3505
body:
The scams that hit older New Yorkers hardest are impostor calls: a fake grandchild in trouble, a fake Social Security or Medicare agent, a fake utility shutoff, or a fake bank or tech support rep. Each one pushes for fast payment by gift card, wire, payment app, cryptocurrency or cash. If money already went out, call the bank first, then the police, then the New York Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755.

The Federal Trade Commission boils every scam down to four signs. The caller pretends to be from someone you know, says there's a problem or a prize, pressures you to act now, and tells you how to pay. Any one of those is a reason to hang up.

How does the grandparent scam work?

Someone calls or texts pretending to be a grandchild or other relative in trouble. The story might be an arrest, a car crash or being stuck in another country. Sometimes a second caller plays a lawyer, police officer or doctor. The New York State Office for the Aging warns that scammers now use artificial intelligence to copy a loved one's voice.

New York's Division of Consumer Protection lists three hallmarks.

  • A family member in trouble. Scammers find names and details on social media, so it helps to check privacy settings.
  • An urgent need for money. Bail, a hospital bill, a fine. The money has to go right now.
  • A demand for secrecy. "Don't tell Mom and Dad." Once your parent calls another relative, the scam usually falls apart.

The Division also warns about a newer version where a courier comes to the house to pick up cash in an envelope. It says several courier pickups were reported across New York State over the past year.

Agree on a family code word. A real grandchild will know it. A voice clone won't.

What do Medicare and Social Security scams look like?

They usually start with a call, text or letter that seems official. The Social Security Office of the Inspector General says Social Security will never do any of the following.

  • Suspend your Social Security number because someone else used it in a crime.
  • Threaten arrest or legal action unless you pay a fine or fee right away.
  • Require payment by gift card, wire transfer, internet currency or mailed cash.
  • Promise a benefit increase in exchange for a payment.
  • Email official letters with your personal information.

If your parent really owes Social Security money, the agency mails a letter with payment options and appeal rights. The Inspector General also warns that scammers may use real names or badge numbers to sound official. Report Social Security scams at oig.ssa.gov.

Medicare says it will never call to sell you anything or come to your home. It only calls asking for personal information in a few cases, such as returning a call your parent made. Tell your mom or dad to share their Medicare number only with their doctors and people they know should have it. Check each Medicare statement against the calendar to make sure every service actually happened.

To report Medicare fraud, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). For a Medicare Advantage or drug plan, your parent can also call the plan fraud line, I-MEDIC, at 1-877-772-3379. Medicare also says not to join a health or drug plan over the phone unless your parent called and asked for help. Our Medicare open enrollment guide explains how to change plans safely.

How do utility shutoff and tech support scams work?

Both rely on fear. A utility scammer says the power or gas goes off in an hour unless your parent pays an overdue bill now. A tech support scammer puts a pop-up on the screen saying the computer is infected, with a number to call.

Utility scams

The New York State Department of Public Service says real utilities send several mailed disconnection notices for past-due bills. They don't demand payment only by gift card, prepaid card, cryptocurrency, wire or payment app. It also warns about fake overpayment refunds, equipment or repair fees, made-up federal bill credits and solar offers that are too good to be true.

The department suggests asking the caller for your account number, last payment amount and date, and their employee ID. Then reach the utility on a phone number you already know is real, such as the one on the bill. If your parent gets help with heating costs, our HEAP guide covers the real program.

Tech support and the "phantom hacker"

The New York Attorney General has warned about a three-step scam aimed at people near or past retirement. First a fake tech support agent gets remote access to the computer and looks over the bank accounts. Then a fake bank employee calls to say the account was hacked and the money must move to a "safe" account, sometimes said to be at the Federal Reserve. Finally a fake government agent calls, or sends a letter on fake letterhead, to make it all seem real.

The Attorney General's advice is simple. Never give a stranger remote access to a computer. Never move money out of a bank account because someone on the phone says to. If someone says there's a problem with an account, hang up and call the number on the bank statement.

What about romance, investment and crypto scams?

These take longer and often cost more. A romance scammer meets your parent on a dating site or app, or on social media. They chat often, say it's true love, but can't meet in person. Then the money requests start: a plane ticket, surgery, a visa, or a way to "help you invest."

The FTC's bottom line is to never send money or gifts to a sweetheart you haven't met in person. It also says that if someone you meet on a dating site or app wants to show you how to invest in crypto, that's a scam.

The FTC says only scammers demand payment in cryptocurrency, and only scammers guarantee profits. Crypto payments usually can't be reversed. A newer twist sends people to a cryptocurrency ATM, with the scammer on the phone giving step-by-step directions and a QR code. That money goes straight to the scammer.

Why gift cards and crypto?

Scammers ask for gift cards, wires, payment apps and crypto because that money is hard to trace and hard to get back. Government agencies and utilities don't demand those. A request to pay that way is the clearest sign of a scam there is.

Where do I report a scam in New York?

Report to more than one place. Each agency handles a different piece, and a police report helps with any recovery later.

What happenedWho to contactHow
Danger right now, or someone at the door for cashPolice911
Any scam or deceptive businessNY Attorney General1-800-771-7755 or online complaint
Banks, insurance, financial exploitationNYS Department of Financial Services1-800-342-3736 or dfs.ny.gov
Consumer problems with a businessNYS Division of Consumer Protection1-800-697-1220, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
A business in the five boroughsNYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)Online complaint form, or by mail to 42 Broadway, New York, NY 10004
Any scam, for national trackingFederal Trade CommissionReportFraud.ftc.gov
Online or internet fraudFBI Internet Crime Complaint Centeric3.gov
Social Security scamsSSA Office of the Inspector Generaloig.ssa.gov
Medicare fraudMedicare1-800-633-4227
Fake utility callsYour utility, and local policeNumber on the real bill
  1. Call the bank or card company first. The Office for the Aging's advice is to contact the financial institution right away to see whether a payment can be stopped. If a gift card or wire was used, the FTC says to call that company too and ask for a refund.
  2. Change passwords. Do this for any account the scammer could see, especially after remote access to a computer.
  3. File a police report. The Office for the Aging says you'll need it to recover money or file other claims.
  4. Report to the Attorney General and the FTC. A report helps them track the scam and warn others.
  5. Gather the paperwork. Keep receipts, texts, call logs, gift card numbers and the names the callers used.

What can banks do, and when does Adult Protective Services step in?

Federal bank regulators and state financial regulators have urged banks to train staff to spot exploitation. They also suggest using transaction holds and payment delays where the law allows, and letting customers name a trusted contact. Ask your parent's bank whether it lets customers name one. That gives the bank someone to call if it sees something odd.

Don't count on the bank to stop a transfer your parent authorized. The FTC's advice is to call the bank right away and ask, but the surest protection is catching the scam before money moves.

When the person taking the money is someone your parent knows, the Department of Financial Services says that is the most common kind of exploitation. Warning signs include unpaid bills, new friends who suddenly get close, sudden changes to a will, trust, insurance or other financial papers, and transfers your parent can't explain.

That is when Adult Protective Services (APS) comes in. APS serves adults with physical or mental impairments who need help protecting themselves.

  • New York City. Call the DSS OneNumber at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and say "APS." Anyone can make a referral. If your parent is eligible for an assessment, a home visit comes within three business days, or 24 hours if the situation is life-threatening.
  • Outside the city. Call the county Department of Social Services, or the statewide APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505.

Our Adult Protective Services guide explains what happens after a report. A power of attorney chosen carefully, with a second person who can check the accounts, is a strong defense for any family.

faq.q: My dad in Queens got a call saying his grandson was in jail and needed bail. What do I do?
faq.a: Have him hang up and call the grandson or another relative directly on a number he knows. If he already paid, call his bank right away, then file a police report and report it to the NY Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755. If someone is coming to the house for cash, call 911.

faq.q: How do I report that my mom in Westchester was scammed out of money?
faq.a: Call her bank first to see if the payment can be stopped. Then file a police report, report to the NY Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755 and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If someone she knows is taking her money, call Westchester County's Department of Social Services for Adult Protective Services.

faq.q: Does Social Security ever call and threaten arrest?
faq.a: No. The Social Security Inspector General says Social Security will never threaten arrest unless you pay right away, suspend your number, or ask for gift cards, wires, internet currency or mailed cash. Report these calls at oig.ssa.gov.

faq.q: Will my utility call and shut off power today unless I pay?
faq.a: The NYS Department of Public Service says real utilities send several mailed disconnection notices first and don't demand payment only by gift card, crypto, wire or payment app. Hang up and call the utility on a number you know is real, such as the one on your bill.

faq.q: Who do I call about Medicare fraud?
faq.a: Call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). For a Medicare Advantage or drug plan, you can also call I-MEDIC at 1-877-772-3379. Medicare says it never calls to sell anything or visits homes.

faq.q: Can the bank get back money sent to a scammer?
faq.a: Sometimes, if you act fast. Call the bank or card company right away and ask them to stop or reverse the payment. Cryptocurrency payments usually can't be reversed, according to the FTC.

title: Senior fares on New York trains, ferries and county buses
seoTitle: Senior Fares on NY Trains, Ferries and Buses
seoDesc: Senior fares on Metro-North, LIRR, NYC Ferry, Bee-Line, NICE, Suffolk and Rockland buses and NJ TRANSIT, with ages, ID rules, peak limits and today's prices.
dek: Half fares start at 60, 62 or 65 depending on the system, and each one has its own ID and rush-hour rules. Here is what Metro-North, the LIRR, the ferries, the county buses and NJ TRANSIT actually charge older riders.
keyFacts: LIRR and Metro-North: half the one-way peak fare at 65, except weekday morning peak trains into the city
Staten Island Ferry is free; NYC Ferry lists a $1.50 discount fare for enrolled riders 65+
Suffolk Transit: 75 cents for riders over 60; TOR rides in Rockland are free for now
NJ TRANSIT: 50% or more off the regular one-way fare at 62, any time of day
OMNY customer service: 877-789-6669, 24/7
body:
Most New York transit systems cut the fare roughly in half for older riders, but the starting age and the ID rules change from one system to the next. The MTA, Metro-North, the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR), NYC Ferry and Westchester's Bee-Line start at 65. Suffolk County Transit and Transport of Rockland start at 60, NJ TRANSIT starts at 62, and the Staten Island Ferry is free for everyone.

This guide puts each system's own rules side by side. It covers what ID to carry, when the discount does not apply, and how to get the MTA Reduced-Fare OMNY card that works on subways, MTA buses and the Bee-Line. Every fare below comes from the operator's own page. Fares change, so check the link before a big trip.

Which senior fare applies where?

SystemWho gets the senior fareSenior fareMain rule
Subway, local and Select buses, Staten Island Railway65 and older, or a qualifying disability$1.50 (half the $3 fare)Reduced-Fare OMNY card; after 12 paid rides in 7 days, the rest are free
MTA express bus65 and older$3.60Not on weekdays 6 to 10 a.m. or 3 to 7 p.m.
LIRR and Metro-North65 and olderHalf the one-way peak fareNot on weekday morning peak trains into the city terminals, 6 to 10 a.m.
Staten Island FerryEveryoneFreeNo ticket needed
NYC Ferry65 and older, after you enroll$1.50 one way (as listed on NYC Ferry's ticketing page in November 2026)Buy in the NYC Ferry app or at the Wall Street/Pier 11 landing
Bee-Line (Westchester)65 and older, certified disabled riders, or Medicare card holders with photo ID$1.50; BxM4C express $3.85BxM4C discount off-peak only
Transport of Rockland (TOR)60 and older$1 (fares are waived for now)Proof of age; $2 photo ID card available
NICE bus (Nassau)65 and older, or Medicare card holders$1.50Government ID, Medicare card, Reduced-Fare OMNY card or Nassau Senior Leisure Pass
Suffolk County TransitOver 6075 centsLicense, state ID or municipal senior ID
NJ TRANSIT62 and older (65 to or from Metro-North stations)50% or more off the regular one-way fareAny time of day
One card in the wallet covers a lot. The Reduced-Fare OMNY card is accepted as senior ID on the subway, MTA buses, the Bee-Line, NICE, both commuter railroads and NJ TRANSIT.

How do seniors ride Metro-North and the LIRR for less?

Riders 65 and older pay half of the one-way peak fare on both railroads. You buy a reduced-fare ticket at a ticket office or on the train, and you show ID when you buy it.

The MTA accepts any one of these as proof:

  • A Reduced-Fare OMNY card or MetroCard. It only serves as ID, so it does not need money on it.
  • A paratransit card, such as Access-A-Ride, Able-Ride or Suffolk County Accessible Transportation (SCAT).
  • A Medicare card. A Medicaid card does not count.
  • A driver's license, birth certificate or passport showing you are over 65.

When can't you use the senior ticket?

On the LIRR, reduced-fare tickets can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal, Hunterspoint Avenue or Long Island City between 6 and 10 a.m. On Metro-North, the same limit applies to weekday morning trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 a.m. Evening peak trains are fine on both.

There is no reduced-fare version of multi-trip tickets. The MTA says a daily commuter can get similar savings with a monthly ticket.

Say your dad lives in White Plains and has a 9:30 a.m. appointment in Midtown. A train that reaches Grand Central at 9:15 needs a full fare. If the doctor can see him at 11, a train arriving after 10 a.m. costs half, and so does the ride home at 5 p.m.

Can someone help my parent board the train?

Yes. Both railroads take call-ahead requests and pass them to the train crew.

  • Metro-North. Call 511 between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., at least 15 minutes before the trip.
  • LIRR. Call 718-547-7227 at least 2 hours before the train leaves. The line is open 24/7. You can also ask in person at Penn Station, Grand Central, Atlantic Terminal or Jamaica, at least 15 minutes ahead.

Personal care attendants ride free on both railroads, though they may be asked for ID showing they work for a PCA agency. Many cars have priority seating marked with the accessibility symbol near the doors. For accessible parking, call 718-217-5477 for the LIRR or 511 for Metro-North. Check elevator and escalator status on the MTA site before you leave home.

How does my parent get the MTA Reduced-Fare OMNY card?

Anyone 65 or older qualifies on age alone, with no income test. The fastest route is in person, where riders 65 and up can often leave with the card the same day.

  1. Bring a photo ID. The MTA accepts a valid driver's license from any state, or a birth certificate or Medicare card paired with a photo ID.
  2. Pick a place. Go to a Customer Service Center inside select accessible subway stations (open 24/7), the center at 3 Stone Street in Lower Manhattan (weekdays, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) or an MTA Mobile Sales van. In Westchester, the Bee-Line runs its own Mobile Sales Van that makes scheduled visits around the county. Call 914-813-7777 for an application.
  3. Apply. Fill out the age application on site. Some applications need more review and won't be finished that day.
  4. Or mail it. Send the age application, a 2 by 1.5 inch passport-style photo and a copy of your ID to MTA New York City Transit, Attn: Reduced Fare Program, 130 Livingston St, Brooklyn, NY 11201-9625. The MTA warns new mail applicants may wait up to three months.
  5. Set up the card. Load money online with a free OMNY account. For card problems, call OMNY at 877-789-6669, 24/7.

The online application is not available right now. Our MTA reduced fare guide covers the disability route and the ID rules in more detail. If your parent can't manage buses or subways at all, see the Access-A-Ride guide instead.

What do the ferries cost older riders?

The Staten Island Ferry costs nothing for anyone. NYC Ferry sells a $1.50 one-way ticket to riders 65 and older, as listed on NYC Ferry's ticketing page in November 2026, but only after they enroll in its Ferry Discount Program.

Staten Island Ferry

NYC DOT runs free service between St. George on Staten Island and Whitehall in Lower Manhattan every day of the week, year-round. There's no ticket and no senior card to show. Questions go to the Passenger Service Office at 212-839-3061.

NYC Ferry

NYC Ferry's ticketing page lists a regular one-way ticket at $5 and the Ferry Discount Program ticket at $1.50. An older section lower on the same page and the NYC Ferry FAQ still show $1.35, so check the ticketing page before you go. To join, apply online or print the form and mail it, and allow up to 30 days for processing. Seniors send one of these to prove age:

  • A government-issued ID, such as a driver's license or REAL ID from any state, IDNYC, a passport from any country, Tribal ID or U.S. military ID
  • A government ID that expired within the past 3 years
  • A birth certificate or adoption papers
  • A Medicare card

Once approved, buy discount tickets in the NYC Ferry app or as paper tickets at the Wall Street/Pier 11 landing. NYC Ferry says the ticket vending machines don't sell reduced fare tickets. Its FAQ lists Pier 11 booth hours of 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. but is not consistent about which days, so call ahead or use the app. Tickets expire 90 days after purchase, and a ticket includes a free transfer to another route within 120 minutes of activation. NYC Ferry says enrollment does not expire for riders who qualify as seniors.

What do county buses charge older riders?

Each county sets its own rules. Here is what the four large systems near the city say on their own pages.

  • Bee-Line, Westchester. The senior fare is $1.50 for riders at least 65, certified disabled riders and Medicare card holders with photo ID. Pay exact cash with a Half-Fare ID card (one transfer included) or tap a personalized Reduced-Fare OMNY card. With OMNY, reduced-fare riders pay at most $17.50 a week. The BxM4C express to Manhattan is $3.85 for seniors off-peak. Bee-Line no longer accepts MetroCard. Call 914-813-7777. See the Westchester County page.
  • Transport of Rockland (TOR). Rockland County says fare collection is waived and TOR and TRIPS rides remain free at this time. When fares return, the senior fare is $1 for riders 60 and older with proof of age. A Reduced-Fare Photo ID card costs $2 from the Department of Public Transportation at 50 Sanatorium Road, Building T, in Pomona. Call the Rockland Transit Information Center at 845-364-3333. See the Rockland County page.
  • NICE, Nassau. The regular fare is $3. Riders 65 and older or with a Medicare card pay $1.50 with a government-issued ID, Medicare card, Reduced-Fare OMNY card or Nassau Senior Leisure Pass. Fareboxes take coins but no dollar bills. NICE also takes OMNY and contactless taps. See the Nassau County page.
  • Suffolk County Transit. The full fare is $2.25. Riders over 60 pay 75 cents with a license, state ID or municipal senior ID card. Medicare card holders also pay 75 cents. Transfers cost 25 cents. The Bus Information Line is 631-852-4880, with interpreters available. See the Suffolk County page.

Rockland also runs TRIPS, a paratransit bus for county residents with disabilities and for eligible seniors. Riders must be pre-certified and pre-registered before they can book, and the cash fare is $3 a ride when fares are collected.

Can my parent get a senior fare on NJ TRANSIT?

Yes, and you don't need to live in New Jersey. NJ TRANSIT says riders 62 and older save 50% or more on a regular one-way fare on its trains, buses and light rail, at any time.

Seniors may be asked for any ID or document printed with their date of birth. NJ TRANSIT lists a Medicare card, a driver's license, a passport, a birth certificate and an MTA Reduced Fare card, among others. On private interstate buses not marked NJ TRANSIT, you also need a Reduced Fare Coupon each time you ride.

Two details matter for New Yorkers. First, on trips to or from Metro-North stations, such as on the Port Jervis Line, Metro-North rules apply and the senior age is 65. Metro-North's number for this is 212-532-4900. Second, since January 1, 2026, NJ TRANSIT no longer accepts its old Reduced Fare ID cards without a photo. NJ TRANSIT's own Reduced Fare card is free and arrives by mail about four weeks after you apply. For language help with the program, call 973-491-7112.

What mistakes cost older riders money?

  • Riding into the city before 10 a.m. on a senior rail ticket. Senior tickets aren't valid on weekday morning peak trains into the city terminals.
  • Buying a 10-trip rail ticket. There's no senior version. Buy one-way reduced tickets instead.
  • Using a regular OMNY tap on the Bee-Line or the subway. The half fare only comes off with a personalized Reduced-Fare OMNY card.
  • Waiting at the NYC Ferry vending machine. Discount tickets are sold in the app or at the Wall Street/Pier 11 landing.
  • Paying for the Staten Island Ferry. It's free, and there is no ticket to buy.
  • Assuming 65 everywhere. In Suffolk and Rockland the senior bus fare starts at 60, and on NJ TRANSIT it starts at 62.

Cheaper fares are one way to stretch a fixed income. If your parent recently stopped driving, our guide for older drivers covers what comes next, and free and discounted programs in New York lists other savings.

faq.q: Can my mom ride the bus for free in Rockland County?
faq.a: Right now, yes. Rockland County says fare collection is waived and Transport of Rockland (TOR) and TRIPS rides are free at this time. When fares return, the TOR senior fare is $1 for riders 60 and older with proof of age. Call 845-364-3333 for current details.

faq.q: How does my dad in Westchester get the senior fare on the Bee-Line?
faq.a: He pays $1.50 if he is at least 65, or holds a Medicare card and shows photo ID. He can pay cash with a Half-Fare ID card or tap a personalized Reduced-Fare OMNY card, which caps his weekly cost at $17.50. Bee-Line no longer takes MetroCard. Call 914-813-7777 for help.

faq.q: Can I use my Medicare card for a discount on the LIRR or Metro-North?
faq.a: Yes. A Medicare card is one of the IDs both railroads accept for a reduced-fare ticket, which is half the one-way peak fare. A Medicaid card is not accepted. The ticket can't be used on weekday morning peak trains arriving at the city terminals between 6 and 10 a.m.

faq.q: Is the Staten Island Ferry free for seniors?
faq.a: It's free for everyone. NYC DOT runs it between St. George and Whitehall every day of the year, and you don't need a ticket or senior ID.

faq.q: How do seniors get the NYC Ferry discount?
faq.a: Riders 65 and older apply to the Ferry Discount Program online or by mail with proof of age, such as a Medicare card or government ID. Processing takes up to 30 days. Once approved, buy discount one-way tickets in the NYC Ferry app or at the Wall Street/Pier 11 landing. NYC Ferry's ticketing page listed them at $1.50 in November 2026.

faq.q: Does NJ TRANSIT give a senior discount to New York residents?

title: Affordable senior housing in New York: how to apply and where
seoTitle: Affordable Senior Housing in New York: How to Apply
seoDesc: Section 202, NYCHA senior buildings, Section 8 and NYC Housing Connect lotteries for New Yorkers 62+. Who qualifies, what rent costs and how to apply.
dek: Low-cost senior apartments in New York come with income limits and long waiting lists. Here is how Section 202, NYCHA, Section 8, Housing Connect and state-financed housing work, and how to get on the lists.
keyFacts: Section 202 serves very low-income households with someone 62+
NYCHA senior buildings: everyone in the household must be 62+
NYCHA rent is 30% of gross income minus deductions
NYCHA and HCR never charge a fee to apply
NYCHA Customer Contact Center: 718-707-7771
body:
Affordable senior housing in New York comes from a handful of public programs: HUD Section 202 buildings for very low-income households with someone 62 or older, NYCHA senior buildings and Section 8 vouchers, NYC Housing Connect lotteries, and state-financed apartments you can search on the HCR website. Most have income limits, and most have waiting lists, so the single most useful step is to apply to several at once.

In most of these programs the tenant pays about 30% of income toward rent. This guide covers who qualifies for each one, how to apply in New York City and the rest of the state, how 55+ communities differ from assisted living, and how to keep rent and taxes down if your parent stays put.

What kinds of affordable senior housing are there in New York?

There are two broad kinds of help. Some programs fund whole buildings, and you apply to the building or its waiting list. Others give the renter a voucher to use with a private landlord.

ProgramWho it servesWhat the tenant paysWhere to apply
HUD Section 202Very low-income households with at least one person 62+Typically 30% of adjusted incomeEach property's owner or manager
NYCHA senior public housingHead or co-head 62+, and all other household members 62+30% of gross income minus deductionsNYCHA self-service portal or 718-707-7771
Section 8 Housing Choice VoucherLow-income households; older adults get a preference on many listsRoughly 30% of income, plus utilitiesNYCHA or HPD in NYC; HCR and its local administrators statewide
NYC Housing Connect lotteriesVaries by building; some lotteries are for applicants 62+Set rent, or 30% of income in some senior buildingsNYC Housing Connect
HCR-financed and Mitchell-Lama housingIncome-limited households; Mitchell-Lama serves middle-income families and seniorsSet by each propertyHousingSearch.ny.gov; in NYC, Mitchell-Lama lists are on NYC Mitchell-Lama Connect

What is HUD Section 202 housing?

Section 202 is a federal program that funds nonprofits to build and run apartment buildings for very low-income people 62 and older. HUD says at least one adult in the household must be 62 or older, and household income must be less than 50% of the area median income (AMI) where the property is.

HUD says residents are typically charged 30% of their adjusted income for rent, and the building receives a Project Rental Assistance Contract that covers reasonable operating costs beyond the tenant's portion. They usually include a service coordinator who links residents to community supports such as cleaning, cooking and transportation, so people can keep living on their own.

There is no single Section 202 application. HUD does not manage leasing, so you apply with each property's owner or manager directly. HUD's online Resource Locator has a search for affordable senior and special needs housing that shows 202 properties near you. Your county Office for the Aging, or NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469, can also help you find senior buildings nearby. Suffolk County's Office for the Aging, for example, keeps a list of federally subsidized housing in the county and notes that waiting lists can be quite long.

Put your parent on several building waiting lists at once. Each list moves on its own.

How do NYCHA senior buildings and Section 8 work in New York City?

NYCHA runs public housing for seniors where the head or co-head of household is at least 62 and everyone else in the household is 62 or older too. Rent is 30% of the household's expected gross annual income, minus deductions, and utilities are included in most buildings.

You apply online at NYCHA's self-service portal (selfserve.nycha.info). If you don't have internet, you can schedule an appointment at a NYCHA walk-in center and use a kiosk, or call the Customer Contact Center at 718-707-7771, weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. You don't submit documents with the application. They are checked later, at an eligibility interview.

A few rules from NYCHA's applicant FAQ are worth knowing:

  • No specific building. You pick a first and second choice of borough, not a development.
  • No minimum income. There is a maximum. The current public housing limit is $95,000 for one person and $108,600 for two.
  • Renew every two years. Your application stays active for 24 months. Renew it on the portal to keep your place, and you keep your original filing date.
  • No estimate of wait time. NYCHA says the waitlist is so large, and vacancies so low, that it can't estimate when you will be called.
  • Accessible apartments exist. NYCHA has 504 apartments for people with mobility impairments or special medical needs.

NYCHA also runs the largest Section 8 program in the country. With a voucher, the household generally pays 30% of adjusted monthly income toward rent and NYCHA pays the rest to the landlord. NYCHA's current Section 8 income limits are $56,700 for one person and $64,800 for two. On NYCHA's Section 8 waitlist, people 62 and older and people with disabilities are the second priority group, after people with mobility impairments living in inaccessible housing. HPD and HCR also run Section 8 programs in the city.

NYCHA warns that it never charges a fee to apply for public housing or Section 8. If someone asks your parent to pay, report it to the NYCHA Inspector General at 212-306-3355.

How do NYC Housing Connect lotteries work for older adults?

NYC Housing Connect is the city's portal for affordable rentals and homeownership across the five boroughs. You register once, then apply to individual lotteries, and applicants are drawn by lottery.

Some lotteries are only for older adults. One past example, a Mitchell-Lama lottery at Manhattan Plaza that closed on December 15, 2025, required applicants to be at least 62 and live in Community Board 4, with rent set at 30% of adjusted household income. Each listing shows the income range, household size and any preferences, such as for people who live in the local community board.

  1. Register. Create a NYC Housing Connect account with your parent's household details and income.
  2. Filter for senior listings. Search by borough, income and household size, and look for 62+ set-asides.
  3. Apply only once per lottery. Duplicate applications can disqualify you. Don't send both a paper and an online entry.
  4. Watch for alerts. Housing Connect sends deadline alerts and lets you upload documents electronically.
  5. Prepare documents. If selected, your parent will need proof of identity, household size and income at an eligibility review.
  6. Keep applying. Each lottery is separate. Applying to many raises the odds.

If the online system is hard to use, the Housing Connect applicant hotline is 212-863-7990. HPD says to leave a voicemail and the team will call back. The Housing Connect listing we checked charged no deposit or application fee. Never pay anyone to enter a lottery.

What about senior housing outside New York City?

Outside the five boroughs, start with two places: HCR's housing search website and the Section 8 office for your county. Then ask the county Office for the Aging for a list of senior buildings.

HousingSearch.ny.gov. New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) runs this free site for affordable housing financed by HCR and its public and private partners. You can filter by location, rent, unit size and amenities, create one profile, and apply to properties online.

Section 8 through HCR. HCR runs the Housing Choice Voucher program through local administrators, usually by county. You can apply online through the MyHousing Portal when a waiting list is open, or on paper with your local administrator. HCR's preferences include households with an older adult or a person with a disability, as HUD defines them, among other groups. A tenant-based voucher usually has to be used within that program's area, often the county line. Being on a NYCHA or HPD list does not put you on an HCR list. You must apply separately. For help, HCR's call center is 833-791-2748.

A few local administrators near New Jersey, from HCR's list:

  • Rockland: Rockland County Department of Social Services, Pomona, 845-364-3330
  • Westchester: CVR New York Westchester HCVP, White Plains, applicant inquiries 914-873-1045
  • Orange: PathStone, Middletown, 845-343-0771
  • Putnam: Putnam County Housing Corporation, Carmel, 845-225-8493
  • Nassau and Suffolk: Community Development Long Island, Melville, 631-471-1215

Many cities and towns also have their own housing authorities with senior buildings. Those keep separate lists, so call them directly.

How is a 55+ community different from assisted living?

A 55+ community is ordinary housing with an age rule. Assisted living is licensed by the state and comes with meals, personal care and supervision.

The federal Fair Housing Act lets qualifying housing for older persons limit residents by age. Housing for people 62 and older must be intended for, and solely occupied by, people 62 or older. For a 55+ community, at least 80% of units must have at least one occupant 55 or older, the community must publish and follow policies showing it intends to be 55+ housing, and it must verify residents' ages under HUD rules. A 55+ community does not have to offer any care at all.

New York's adult care facilities are different. They are licensed by the state and overseen by the Department of Health. NYC311 describes the main types this way:

  • Adult homes provide three meals a day, housekeeping, personal care, social activities and 24-hour supervision, but not nursing care.
  • Enriched housing programs are apartments, mainly for people 65 and older, with one or two daily group meals, light personal care, housekeeping, shopping help and care management.
  • Assisted Living Programs add home health aide services, intermittent nursing and therapy for eligible residents of certain licensed adult homes or enriched housing.

You can compare licensed facilities on NYS Health Profiles, the state health department's public site. Our guide to caring for an aging parent walks through how to choose. For complaints about an adult care facility, the Department of Health's intake line is 1-866-893-6772. If your parent needs nursing care around the clock, see our nursing home ratings guide.

What if my parent wants to stay where they are?

Staying put is often the cheapest choice, and several programs help with that. Renters in rent-stabilized apartments may qualify for a rent freeze, and homeowners can cut property taxes.

  • Rent freeze (NYC). NYC Aging says SCRIE can freeze rent for heads of household 62 and older with household income of $50,000 or less whose rent is more than one-third of income. See our SCRIE and DRIE guide.
  • Property tax help. See the senior citizens homeowners exemption and Enhanced STAR.
  • Eviction help (NYC). NYC Aging's Tenancy and Eviction Support Services helps older adults facing eviction in Manhattan, Brooklyn or Bronx housing court. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.
  • Safety changes at home. Grab bars, ramps and repairs can make a home workable for years longer. See our home modifications guide.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Applying to just one list. NYCHA, HPD, HCR and each Section 202 building keep separate lists.
  • Letting an application lapse. Update the address and phone number whenever they change, and renew NYCHA every two years.
  • Paying anyone to apply. NYCHA and HCR never charge application fees.
  • Confusing "senior housing" with care. A 55+ building has no aides. Ask what services, if any, come with the rent.

faq.q: How do I get my mom on a waiting list for senior housing in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Apply to several programs at once. File a NYCHA public housing application online at selfserve.nycha.info (or call 718-707-7771 for a paper one), register on NYC Housing Connect and apply to lotteries with 62+ set-asides, and contact Section 202 buildings in Brooklyn directly. Each list is separate.

faq.q: How can my dad find low-income senior apartments in Westchester?
faq.a: Search HousingSearch.ny.gov for HCR-financed properties, call the county's Section 8 administrator (CVR New York Westchester HCVP, applicant inquiries 914-873-1045) when its list is open, and ask the Westchester Department of Senior Programs and Services and local housing authorities for senior building lists.

faq.q: How long is the wait for NYCHA senior housing?
faq.a: NYCHA says it cannot estimate when you will be called because the waitlist is very large and vacancies are low. Applicants who live or work in New York City are prioritized. Keep the application current and renew it every two years.

faq.q: What is the income limit for Section 202 senior housing?
faq.a: Section 202 is for very low-income households, and HUD says household income must be less than 50% of the area median income where the property is. The dollar limit depends on the county and household size, and rent is typically 30% of adjusted income. Ask the property's manager for its current limits.

faq.q: Is a 55+ community the same as assisted living in New York?
faq.a: No. A 55+ community is regular housing that meets federal age rules, such as at least 80% of units having an occupant 55 or older. Adult homes and assisted living are licensed by the state, overseen by the Department of Health, and provide meals, personal care and supervision.

faq.q: Can I apply for both NYCHA public housing and Section 8?
faq.a: Yes. NYCHA lets you apply for both, but you can only receive one at a time. If you are selected for one, your priority on the other list is significantly reduced. HCR's Section 8 lists are separate and require their own application.

title: Senior transportation in Orange County, NY: every ride, town by town
seoTitle: Senior Transportation in Orange County, NY
seoDesc: Every ride for older adults in Orange County, NY: Dial-A-Ride by town, senior buses, $0.75 bus and paratransit fares, Medicaid rides and the Port Jervis Line.
dek: Orange County has no single senior bus. It has Dial-A-Ride in eleven towns, villages and cities, a few free or donation senior buses, three local bus systems and a train into New Jersey. Here is what serves each town and what it costs.
keyFacts: Dial-A-Ride serves 11 Orange County towns, villages and cities; book at least 24 hours ahead
Senior Dial-A-Ride fares run from $0.50 to $2.00 in most towns
Local buses in Newburgh and Middletown charge seniors $0.75
ADA Paratransit costs $0.75 one way; applications at 845-615-3850
Medicaid rides to medical visits: Medical Answering Services, 866-932-7740
body:
In Orange County, the ride an older adult can get depends almost entirely on the town they live in. Dial-A-Ride buses serve eleven towns, villages and cities, with senior fares of $0.50 to $2.00 in most of them, and several also run a separate senior bus that is free or asks a $1 donation.

Add the $0.75 senior fare on the Newburgh, Middletown and Kiryas Joel local buses, ADA Paratransit, Medicaid rides and the Port Jervis Line into New Jersey, and most parts of the county have something. The gaps are real, though, so the town table below is the place to start.

What ride options does an older adult in Orange County have?

  • Town Dial-A-Ride (Dial-A-Bus). Curb-to-curb shared rides, open to the public, booked at least 24 hours ahead. Seniors pay a reduced fare.
  • Town senior buses. Separate buses for residents 60 and older in Blooming Grove, Montgomery and Crawford, the City of Middletown and the Town of Newburgh.
  • Local buses. Fixed routes in and around Newburgh, Middletown and Kiryas Joel. Seniors pay $0.75 on local trips.
  • ADA Paratransit. For people whose disability keeps them off the local bus, within three quarters of a mile of a bus route, for $0.75.
  • Medicaid transportation. Free rides to medical appointments for Medicaid members.
  • Port Jervis Line and NJ TRANSIT buses. Trains from seven Orange County stations into New Jersey, and buses from Warwick.

The county's Transit Orange trip planner pulls these services together. For questions, call the Orange County Department of Planning at 845-615-3850.

Which ride options serve each Orange County town?

Fares below are the senior fares. Where a town's own page and the Transit Orange page differ, we use the town's page and note it. Call to confirm before the first ride.

Town, city or villageDial-A-Ride (senior fare, phone)Senior bus or other
Blooming Grove (Washingtonville, South Blooming Grove)None listedSenior bus for residents over 60, $1 donation each way, 24 hours notice: 845-496-4411
ChesterGoshen and Chester Dial-A-Ride, $2.00: 845-294-8920
GoshenGoshen and Chester Dial-A-Ride, $2.00: 845-294-8920Warwick buses also reach the Government Center
Highlands (Highland Falls, Fort Montgomery)Half fare ($0.50) for 60+, disabled riders and Medicare card holders on the $1.00 Dial-A-Bus: 845-446-7433Saturday trip to Vails Gate stores if 5 sign up
Kiryas Joel and Palm TreeVillage Dial-A-Ride, 65+ pay $1.50 inside the village, $3.00 outside: 845-492-3287Local bus, 60+ pay $0.75 inside, $1.50 outside: 845-783-8300
Middletown (city)None; Wallkill Dial-A-Bus serves the town outside the citySenior Shuttle for city residents 60+, $1 suggested: 845-346-4070. Local bus $0.75
Monroe (Monroe village, Harriman) and WoodburyTown Dial-A-Ride, $1.00 for 55+ with verification, per the town page (Transit Orange lists a $1.00 senior fare): 845-783-6222Express Loop fixed route, no reservation
Montgomery and Crawford (Walden, Maybrook, Pine Bush)Dial-A-Bus, $0.50: 845-457-2622Free Senior Bus for 60+, two medical runs a month to Middletown
Newburgh (city) and New WindsorNone listedNewburgh local bus, $0.75: 845-565-7900
Newburgh (town)Dial-A-Bus, $0.50: 845-564-6084Senior Van, $1 suggested each stop: 845-564-7815
Port Jervis (and 3 miles into Deerpark)City Dial-A-Ride, $0.50: 845-856-7999Port Jervis train station
Wallkill (outside Middletown)Dial-A-Bus, $1.00 for 60+, disabled and Medicare: 845-692-7852Middletown local bus reaches Route 211 shopping
Warwick (Florida, Greenwood Lake, Pine Island)Dial-A-Ride, $1.00 for 60+, disabled and Medicare: 845-986-2877Village shuttle 7 days; NJ TRANSIT buses 196 and 197
CornwallNone listed by Transit OrangeSalisbury Mills/Cornwall train station; Newburgh local bus stops at Cornwall Hospital
TuxedoNone listed by Transit OrangeTuxedo train station

More on each town, including senior centers, is on the Orange County page.

How does Dial-A-Ride work in each town?

Dial-A-Ride is a shared bus that picks your parent up at the curb and drops them at the curb. It is not a taxi, so expect other stops along the way. Drivers cannot use driveways or private roads in Monroe or Warwick, and in Warwick drivers cannot help once a rider is off the bus. Book with a live dispatcher unless the town says otherwise.

Goshen and Chester

Rides must start in the Town of Goshen or Chester and stay in those two towns. The bus runs 8 am to 5 pm weekdays. Call 8 am to noon, up to a week ahead. There are no standing appointments, and no weekend calls.

Monroe

The town page lists bus hours of 6 am to 6 pm weekdays and Saturday by reservation only. Transit Orange shows shorter Friday hours, so call to confirm. Phones are answered weekdays 8 am to 3:30 pm. Book three days ahead if you can, never more than a week. Cancel with 24 hours notice. A monthly trip runs to Crystal Run and the Galleria in Wallkill on the last Friday.

Warwick

The town page lists Dial-A-Ride weekdays 8 am to 4:30 pm. Transit Orange lists different hours, so call to confirm. Call 8 am to 2 pm, at least 24 hours and up to a week ahead (3 to 5 days is better). Bring exact change. The bus also makes set-day trips to Monroe and Harriman (first and third Fridays), Goshen, and Middletown shopping and medical centers. Out-of-town runs can be canceled for low ridership.

Wallkill

The town page says buses run 7:30 am to 5 pm weekdays and 8 am to 3:15 pm Saturday (Transit Orange lists an 8 am weekday start). Book by phone 8 am to 2 pm on weekdays, or online. Monday rides must be booked by 1 pm Friday. Tell the dispatcher about a wheelchair lift. Cancel at least 2 hours before pickup. The driver waits 3 minutes.

Montgomery and Crawford, Highlands, Town of Newburgh, Port Jervis

  • Montgomery and Crawford: call 9 am to noon weekdays, at least a day ahead. The village page also prints 845-457-1622 for reservations, so try 845-457-2622 first.
  • Highlands: weekdays 8 am to 4 pm, last pickup 3:45 pm. Reserve 24 hours ahead. No Sunday service.
  • Town of Newburgh: weekdays 8:30 am to 3 pm. Book 24 hours to 14 days ahead, 8 am to noon. No same-day rides.
  • Port Jervis: the bus runs 6 am to 3:30 pm weekdays. Call by noon the business day before (by Friday noon for Monday).

Which senior buses are free or by donation?

  • Blooming Grove Senior Bus. Home pickup for residents over 60, including Washingtonville. Mondays and Wednesdays go to Crystal Run Monroe and Monroe and Woodbury shopping. Tuesdays and Thursdays go to Crystal Run Newburgh, Montefiore Cornwall and Vails Gate and Newburgh stores. Fridays go to Middletown and Goshen doctors and the Galleria. Trips can be canceled if few sign up.
  • Town of Montgomery Senior Bus. Free for people 60 and older, with a donation encouraged. It makes monthly trips out of town and two medical runs a month to Crystal Run Road, Middletown Medical, Orange Radiology and Horton Hospital.
  • City of Middletown Senior Shuttle. Door to door for city residents 60 and older, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm and Sundays 8 am to 12:30 pm, for a $1 suggested donation.
  • Town of Newburgh Senior Van. Curb-to-curb rides for town seniors to recreation programs and shopping, run with the county Office for the Aging, weekdays 8:15 am to 3 pm. Book 24 hours to 14 days ahead. No service when the Newburgh school district closes or delays for weather.
A senior bus that runs only on Tuesdays is still a ride. Ask for the weekly schedule and plan doctor visits around it.

What do local buses and paratransit cost?

Seniors pay $0.75 on the Newburgh and Middletown local buses, and Medicare card holders pay the same on Middletown's buses. Middletown's four routes run Monday to Saturday, 7 am to 5:30 pm, to Garnet Health Medical Center, Crystal Run Healthcare, SUNY Orange and the Galleria. Call 1-800-631-8405. Newburgh routes reach St. Luke's and Cornwall hospitals, Vails Gate and the Newburgh Mall. Neither runs on major holidays.

ADA Paratransit is for people whose disability keeps them from using the local bus for some or all trips. Your parent must apply and get an ADA Paratransit ID card from the county. Call the Department of Planning at 845-615-3850 for an application. Rides cost $0.75 one way and must start and end within three quarters of a mile of a Newburgh, Middletown or Kiryas Joel local bus route. Reserve at least a day ahead.

  • Newburgh area: 845-567-0013
  • Middletown area: 845-467-6641
  • Monroe area: 845-395-3083

Visitors certified for ADA paratransit elsewhere can use the service while in Orange County.

How do Medicaid members get rides to the doctor?

New York pays for non-emergency rides to medical appointments for Medicaid members. Medical Answering Services (MAS) books them. For Orange County, call 866-932-7740, or book at medanswering.com, at least 72 hours ahead. Every trip must be approved first. MAS picks the ride type: public transit, taxi, ambulette, ambulance or mileage paid back for a personal car. Trips to pharmacies or grocery stores are not covered. See our Medicaid guide to check eligibility.

What do seniors pay to get into New Jersey?

On the Port Jervis Line, riders 65 and older pay half the regular one-way fare. The line stops at Port Jervis, Otisville, Middletown/Town of Wallkill, Campbell Hall, Salisbury Mills/Cornwall, Harriman and Tuxedo, then runs through Suffern to Mahwah, Ramsey, Ridgewood, Paterson, Secaucus Junction and Hoboken. Show a Medicare card or any government or transit ID with a birth date. The line timetable says seniors with ID who buy on board skip the $5 surcharge. NJ TRANSIT says Metro-North fare policies apply on this line, and Metro-North bars reduced fares on weekday morning trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 am. Neither page says how that applies here, so call Metro-North at 212-532-4900, the number NJ TRANSIT gives, before a weekday morning trip.

From Warwick and Greenwood Lake, NJ TRANSIT buses 196 and 197 run to New York City, with a free Park and Ride on Route 17A. On NJ TRANSIT buses the senior age is 62, and the fare is half the regular one-way fare at any time. You do not need to live in New Jersey. For subway and bus discounts in the city, see our MTA Reduced-Fare guide.

How do you book a first ride?

  1. Find your parent's town in the table. Note the Dial-A-Ride number and any senior bus.
  2. Call during booking hours. Most offices take calls only in the morning or early afternoon on weekdays. Have the pickup address, destination and appointment time ready.
  3. Ask about proof of age. Several towns need half-fare verification. A Medicare card works in Warwick, Wallkill and Highlands.
  4. Bring exact change. Drivers in Monroe and Warwick cannot make change.
  5. Book the return trip in the same call. Dial-A-Ride is shared, so leave extra time before appointments.
  6. Apply for ADA Paratransit or Medicaid rides if the bus will not work. Call 845-615-3850 for the paratransit application, or MAS at 866-932-7740 for Medicaid trips.
Giving up the car

Try a Dial-A-Ride trip together while your parent still drives, so the switch is less of a shock. Our guide to older drivers in New York covers license renewal and vision rules.

faq.q: How can my mom in Warwick get to her doctor if she stops driving?
faq.a: The Town of Warwick Dial-A-Ride picks up curb to curb on weekdays for $1.00 for riders 60 and older, disabled riders and Medicare card holders, with exact change. Call 845-986-2877 between 8 am and 2 pm, at least 24 hours and up to a week ahead. The bus also runs set-day trips to Middletown medical centers and Monroe. If she has Medicaid, Medical Answering Services (866-932-7740) arranges free rides to medical visits.

faq.q: Is there a senior bus for my dad in Washingtonville?
faq.a: Yes. The Blooming Grove Senior Bus serves residents over 60 in the Town of Blooming Grove, including Washingtonville and South Blooming Grove. It picks up at home and goes to doctors and shopping on set days of the week. Call 845-496-4411 at least 24 hours ahead. A $1 donation each way is requested.

faq.q: What is the senior fare on Dial-A-Ride in Orange County?
faq.a: It depends on the town: $0.50 in Montgomery and Crawford, Highlands, the Town of Newburgh and Port Jervis; $1.00 in Monroe, Wallkill and Warwick; $2.00 in Goshen and Chester; and, for riders 65 and older in Kiryas Joel, $1.50 inside the village and $3.00 outside it.

faq.q: Who can use Transit Orange ADA Paratransit?
faq.a: People whose disability keeps them from using the local bus for some or all trips. You must apply and get an ADA Paratransit ID card from Orange County; call 845-615-3850. Rides cost $0.75 one way and must start and end within three quarters of a mile of a local bus route.

faq.q: Does my parent in Middletown have a door-to-door ride?
faq.a: Yes. The City of Middletown Senior Shuttle gives door-to-door rides to city residents 60 and older, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm and Sundays 8 am to 12:30 pm, for a $1 suggested donation. Call 845-346-4070. The city's local buses charge seniors $0.75.

faq.q: What does the Port Jervis Line cost for seniors?
faq.a: Riders 65 and older pay half the regular one-way fare with a Medicare card or other ID showing their birth date. Seniors with ID who buy on the train skip the $5 surcharge. Call Metro-North at 212-532-4900 to confirm the rule for weekday morning trains.
