seoTitle: Senior Transportation in Rockland County, NY
seoDesc: Every ride for older adults in Rockland: TRIPS, free TOR buses for now, Clarkstown Mini Trans, Medicaid rides, train fares into NJ, and a town-by-town chart.
dek: Rockland has a county senior bus, free TOR buses right now, a Clarkstown town bus and trains into New Jersey. Here is what each one costs, who can ride, and which towns it reaches.
keyFacts: TRIPS serves Rockland residents 60 and older who find the regular bus hard to use
TOR and TRIPS fares are waived and rides are free for now, the county says
TRIPS takes ride requests 7:30 am to 5 pm weekdays at 845-364-8747, up to 14 days ahead
Clarkstown Mini Trans senior and disabled fare is $0.40
Medicaid rides to medical visits: Medical Answering Services, 866-932-7740, 72 hours ahead
body:
An older adult in Rockland County who stops driving has more ride options than most families know about. The county's TRIPS bus picks up residents 60 and older who find the regular bus hard to use, and right now Transport of Rockland (TOR) and TRIPS rides are free because the county has waived fares.

On top of that, Clarkstown runs its own Mini Trans bus for $0.40, Meals on Wheels of Rockland brings people to its lunch centers, Medicaid pays for rides to medical visits, and five Rockland train stations put your parent on a direct line into Bergen County, New Jersey. This page puts them all in one place, with a chart of which options reach each town.

What ride options does an older adult in Rockland have?

There are six. Most families end up using two or three of them together.

  • TRIPS paratransit. The county's shared-ride, curb-to-curb bus, by appointment. Regular TRIPS is open to residents 60 and older who find fixed-route buses difficult or impossible. ADA TRIPS is a stricter service for people certified as unable to use the bus because of a disability.
  • Transport of Rockland (TOR). The county's local bus system. Riders 60 and older get a senior fare, and the county currently lists rides as free.
  • Clarkstown Mini Trans. A Town of Clarkstown bus with five routes that meet at the Nanuet Mall, plus door-to-door rides for Clarkstown senior clubs.
  • Meals on Wheels of Rockland senior activity centers. Weekday lunch centers with rides for a suggested $2 a day.
  • Medicaid transportation. Free rides to medical appointments for Medicaid members, booked through the state's broker.
  • Trains into New Jersey. The Pascack Valley and Port Jervis lines stop in Rockland and run through Bergen and Passaic counties to Secaucus and Hoboken.
For a parent who can still walk to a bus stop, the cheapest ride in Rockland today is a free TOR bus.

Which ride options serve each Rockland town?

TRIPS covers the whole county, so every town has at least that. The rest depends on where your parent lives. The Meals on Wheels column uses the centers that Meals on Wheels of Rockland lists.

Haverstraw (Haverstraw village, West Haverstraw)Yes, countywideNo bus posted; the senior club posts yearly trip lists (Town Hall 845-429-2200)Haverstraw centerNo Rockland station; TOR or TRIPS to Nanuet or Pearl River
Orangetown (Pearl River, Tappan, Piermont, Orangeburg)Yes, countywideNo town bus postedOrangetown center; Nyack centerPearl River station, Pascack Valley Line

Stony PointYes, countywideNo bus posted; senior clubs (55+) meet weekly at Patriot Hills (Recreation 845-947-5261)None listed in Stony PointNo Rockland station; TOR or TRIPS to a station

TOR buses run across the county, but routes change and some streets have detours right now. Check the route map on the county's transit alerts page or call the Transit Information Center at 845-364-3333. Your parent's own town and village pages are on the Rockland County page.

How does TRIPS work for seniors?

TRIPS is a shared van, booked ahead, that picks your parent up at the curb and drops them at the curb of their destination. All vehicles are wheelchair accessible. Other riders may be picked up along the way.

Who can ride

Regular TRIPS is for Rockland residents 60 and older, and residents with physical, developmental or mental disabilities, who find fixed-route buses difficult or impossible to use. It covers all of Rockland, including areas more than three quarters of a mile from a bus route, but those rides are on a space-available basis, so book early.

Hours and fares

Regular TRIPS runs 7 am to 7 pm, Monday to Friday, with limited Saturday service from 8 am to 5 pm. There is no Sunday service, and no service on the holidays the county lists, including Thanksgiving and Christmas. The standard cash fare is $3 each way, or $25 for a book of 10 tickets. The county says fare collection on TOR and TRIPS is waived for now and gives no end date, so ask about the fare when you book.

How to apply

Seniors fill out the Regular TRIPS Application for Seniors. Get it from the Office for the Aging or the Department of Public Transportation, download it from the county's TRIPS application page, or apply in person at Building T of the Dr. Robert L. Yeager Health Center in Pomona, weekdays 9 am to 5 pm. Once approved, your parent pays $2 for a numbered photo ID card and gets a packet that explains how to reserve. For help with the application, the county lists 845-364-2065.

How booking works

Call 845-364-8747 Monday to Friday, 7:30 am to 5 pm, and speak to a staff member. Voicemail requests are not honored. You can request a ride up to 14 days ahead, and the county recommends at least 48 hours (two business days). Have the trip date, full destination address, arrival time and expected length of stay ready. For a medical trip, add the doctor's name and phone. Write down the pickup and return windows they give you.

Cancel more than an hour before the pickup window to avoid a late cancellation. The bus waits two minutes. Three no-shows or late cancellations in 30 days can lead to a suspension. Drivers help with boarding and seat belts but cannot help between the curb and the door, so a parent who needs that help should bring an aide. Tell TRIPS about the aide when you book.

Are Transport of Rockland buses free for seniors right now?

Yes, for now. The county's fares page and transit alerts both say fare collection continues to be waived and rides on TOR and TRIPS remain free, with no end date given. Check the alerts page before relying on it for a regular trip.

When fares come back, the listed TOR senior and disabled fare is $1.00, half the $2.00 cash fare, with a $0.50 senior transfer. Riders 60 and older qualify with valid proof of age. Medicare card holders of any age can show the card for the discount. Rockland residents can get a $2.00 Reduced-Fare Photo ID from the Department of Public Transportation, which saves digging for a birth date at the farebox.

For trips across the Hudson, Hudson Link buses charge riders 60 and older a $1.35 senior fare with a valid ID showing age. A senior ticket with a transfer costs $1.85, and the transfer to TOR, Mini Trans or the Bee-Line is good for two hours.

What other town and nonprofit rides are there?

Clarkstown Mini Trans

Mini Trans runs five routes, A to E, that all meet at the Nanuet Mall, where riders can switch to another Mini Trans route or to TOR. It runs Monday to Friday 6:55 am to 8:05 pm and Saturday 9 am to 7:10 pm, with no Sunday service. The senior and disabled fare is $0.40 cash, with $0.15 transfers. The town also gives weekday door-to-door rides to Clarkstown senior clubs, rides from senior complexes to local supermarkets with help carrying bags in, and rides to monthly senior dance socials. Call 845-623-0667.

Meals on Wheels of Rockland lunch centers

Meals on Wheels of Rockland runs senior activity centers for Clarkstown/Pearl River, Nyack, Orangetown, Ramapo and Haverstraw, generally Monday to Friday, 10 am to 2 pm. The suggested donation is $4 a day for lunch and $2 a day for transportation, and the agency says no one is denied access because of money. Call the main office at 845-624-6325 to ask about a ride to your parent's nearest center.

Rides for veterans

The county's disability office lists veteran transportation to the VA campuses at Montrose and Castle Point through Bridges at 845-624-1366, ext. 102.

The Office for the Aging's volunteer program (RSVP) is recruiting drivers for its Independence Project, which takes older adults to medical appointments and pharmacies. Ask the Office for the Aging main desk at 845-364-2110 whether a volunteer ride is available in your parent's area. It is also the place to start for other help at home through NY Connects.

How do Medicaid members get free rides to the doctor?

If your parent has Medicaid, New York pays for non-emergency rides to medical appointments, including primary care and the dentist. The state's broker, Medical Answering Services (MAS), schedules every trip. For Rockland, the number is 866-932-7740, or book online at medanswering.com.

  • Call at least 72 hours before the appointment. Every trip must be approved first.
  • MAS picks the ride type based on need: public transit, taxi, ambulette, ambulance or mileage paid back for a personal car. Most people travel the way they get around day to day.
  • Medicaid does not pay for trips to pharmacies, gyms or grocery stores. For an emergency, call 911.
  • Fidelis members in Rockland: since April 1, 2026, MAS handles your transportation too, at the same number.

Not sure your parent qualifies? Our Medicaid guide for older New Yorkers covers income limits and how to apply.

What do seniors pay on trains into New Jersey?

Seniors 65 and older pay half the regular one-way fare on NJ TRANSIT trains to and from Rockland's stations. These lines are run by NJ TRANSIT for Metro-North, which is why the age is 65 here. Elsewhere on NJ TRANSIT the senior age is 62.

  • Pascack Valley Line: Spring Valley, Nanuet and Pearl River, then Montvale, Park Ridge, Westwood, Oradell, Hackensack, Secaucus Junction and Hoboken.
  • Port Jervis Line: Suffern and Sloatsburg, then Mahwah, Ramsey, Ridgewood, Paterson, Passaic, Secaucus Junction and Hoboken.

Any government or transit ID with a birth date works, including a Medicare card, an MTA Reduced-Fare card or a driver's license. The line timetables say seniors who buy on board with proper ID skip the $5 on-board surcharge. NJ TRANSIT says riders 62 and older can use the reduced fare at any time, but it sets 65 as the age for trips to or from Metro-North stations and says Metro-North fare policies apply on the Port Jervis Line. Metro-North bars reduced fares on weekday morning trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 am. Neither page spells out how that applies to these trains, so call Metro-North at 212-532-4900, the number NJ TRANSIT gives, before a weekday morning trip.

The county Office for the Aging and the Department of Public Transportation also hand out NJ TRANSIT reduced fare coupons, which private interstate buses not marked NJ TRANSIT require on each ride. For subway and bus discounts once your parent reaches the city, see our MTA Reduced-Fare guide.

How do you book a first ride?

  1. Pick the right service. Can your parent walk to a bus stop and wait? Try TOR or Mini Trans. If not, apply for TRIPS. If they have Medicaid and the trip is medical, call MAS.
  2. Apply for TRIPS before you need it. Fill out the senior application and bring it to Building T in Pomona. Approval comes with a $2 photo ID and a rider packet.
  3. Get the reduced-fare ID. Ask the Department of Public Transportation for the $2 Reduced-Fare Photo ID for TOR, in case fares return.
  4. Call TRIPS two business days ahead. Dial 845-364-8747 between 7:30 am and 5 pm on a weekday. Give the address, arrival time and how long the visit will last.
  5. Write down the pickup window. Have your parent ready at the curb at the start of it. The bus waits two minutes.
  6. Plan the return. Book the ride home in the same call and note the return window.
When a parent stops driving

Set up the ride options before the car keys go away. A parent who has already ridden TRIPS once with you is far more likely to use it alone. Our guide to older drivers in New York covers license renewal and how to talk about it.

If he has Medicaid, Medical Answering Services (866-932-7740) arranges free rides to medical visits with 72 hours notice.

title: Senior transportation in Westchester: every ride option, town by town
seoTitle: Senior Transportation in Westchester County, NY
seoDesc: Every ride for older adults in Westchester: Bee-Line $1.50 senior fare, ParaTransit rules, town senior buses, free medical rides, Metro-North and Medicaid.
dek: Westchester has a half-price Bee-Line fare, a $5 ParaTransit van, and more than 20 town and village senior ride programs that many families never hear about. Here is who runs what, what it costs and how to book.
keyFacts: Bee-Line reduced fare is $1.50 for riders 65+, people with disabilities and Medicare card holders
Bee-Line ParaTransit costs $5 a trip and runs within 3/4 mile of a Bee-Line route
Book ParaTransit at 914-995-7272, weekdays 9 am to 5 pm, up to 7 days ahead
Metro-North reduced fare (65+) is half the peak fare, except weekday trains reaching Grand Central 6 to 10 am
Medicaid rides to medical visits: Medical Answering Services, 844-666-6270
body:
In Westchester, an older adult who stops driving can ride the Bee-Line bus for $1.50 at 65 or older, or use Bee-Line ParaTransit for $5 a trip if a disability keeps them off the bus. Many towns and villages also run their own senior bus, van or taxi coupons, and those are often the easiest ride of all for shopping and doctor visits close to home.

The trouble is that the town programs are scattered across dozens of town and village websites, each with its own phone, days and rules. This page pulls them together with the county and state options, so you can see in one table what your parent can use where they live.

What ride options does an older adult in Westchester have?

  • Bee-Line bus. Close to 60 routes, the county says, in and around Westchester, to the Bronx, Manhattan and Putnam. The reduced fare is half price.
  • Bee-Line ParaTransit. A shared van, booked ahead, for people who are functionally unable to use the regular bus. Age alone does not qualify.
  • Town and village senior transportation. Buses, vans, medical rides and taxi coupons run by local senior and recreation departments, usually for residents 60 and older.
  • TRA free medical rides. A nonprofit, listed by the county, that drives adults 60 and older to medical appointments at no charge.
  • Medicaid transportation. Free rides to medical visits for Medicaid members.
  • Metro-North. Half the peak fare for riders 65 and older on most trains.

Which ride options serve each Westchester town?

Bee-Line ParaTransit (914-995-7272) covers any address within three quarters of a mile of a Bee-Line route in every town below. This table shows the local program each town or village posts. Phones come from the town's own page or the county's 2026 Planning for Driving Retirement guide. Where a town lists rides but no details, call and ask.

Town pages change often, so call before you count on a ride. You can find more on your parent's town on the Westchester County page.

What does the Bee-Line cost for seniors?

The Bee-Line reduced fare is $1.50 a ride, half the $3.00 base fare that took effect January 4, 2026. It is for riders 65 and older, certified disabled riders and anyone with a valid Medicare card.

  • Cash: $1.50, which includes one transfer. Ask for it when you pay.
  • Reduced-Fare OMNY card: $1.50 a tap, with free transfers within two hours to local Bee-Line buses, NYC buses and subways. After 12 rides in 7 days ($17.50 reduced), the rest of that week is free.
  • BxM4C express to Manhattan: the reduced fare is $3.85, off-peak only.

To get a Half-Fare ID card, call the Bee-Line at 914-813-7777 for an application or visit the Mobile Sales Van on its scheduled stops. Bring proof of age and a photo ID. For a parent nervous about the bus, the county's Senior B.E.A.T. (Be Educated About Transit) program teaches how to ride safely. Call 914-995-1621. Our MTA Reduced-Fare guide covers the card in more detail.

Who qualifies for Bee-Line ParaTransit, and how does it work?

ParaTransit is for people who are functionally unable to use the regular Bee-Line bus. A disability by itself does not qualify someone, and neither does age. The county asks two things. Can your parent get to and from a stop? Can they board, ride and get off the bus?

Eligibility types

  • Unconditional: unable to use the regular bus in any circumstance.
  • Conditional: able to use the bus for some trips, with ParaTransit decided trip by trip.
  • Temporary: for a short-term disability, up to 12 months.

Applying

Call 914-995-7272 and press 3 to ask for an application. Fill it in completely, because the decision rests mostly on what you submit. If your parent is found not eligible, the county sends written notice within 21 business days. You can appeal in writing within 60 days. If your parent needs an attendant, note it on the application. One attendant rides free when help is needed. Companions pay a fare.

Fare, area and hours

The fare is $5.00 a trip, exact fare or a ticket. Service runs only within three quarters of a mile of a regular Bee-Line route, and only during the hours that route runs. So a parent on a quiet road far from a bus line, or needing a ride after the route stops for the night, may not be covered.

Booking

Call 914-995-7272, press 1, Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm. Book up to 7 days ahead. Next-day rides must be booked by 5 pm. You can also book online through the county's ParaTransit self-service site or the ParaTransit app. Expect a 30-minute pickup window. The van waits only 5 minutes. Cancel at least 2 hours before the trip (press 2). Standing orders for regular trips must be renewed each quarter, between the 1st and 15th of March, June, September and December.

Check the three-quarter-mile rule first. It decides whether ParaTransit can reach your parent's door at all.

Are there free rides to medical appointments?

Yes, a few. The county lists TRA (Transportation, Resources, Access), a nonprofit that gives free non-emergency medical rides to adults 60 and older anywhere in Westchester, Putnam and southwest Fairfield County. Book Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm, at 914-764-3533. Staff and volunteer drivers do the driving.

Town medical rides fill the same gap closer to home: Eastchester, Pelham, Somers, Scarsdale vouchers and the Sleepy Hollow van all appear in the table above. For cancer treatment, the county guide also lists the American Cancer Society's Road to Recovery volunteer rides at 1-800-227-2345, for patients who can walk to the car or bring a helper.

How do Medicaid members get rides to the doctor?

New York pays for non-emergency rides to medical appointments for Medicaid members. The state's broker, Medical Answering Services (MAS), books them. Westchester is in the downstate region, so call 844-666-6270, or book online at medanswering.com.

  • Call at least 72 hours before the appointment. Every trip must be approved first.
  • MAS chooses the ride type based on need: public transit, taxi, ambulette, ambulance or mileage paid back for a personal car.
  • Medicaid does not cover trips to pharmacies, gyms or grocery stores.

The county's driving guide lists a different MAS number. The state Health Department page is the program's own source, so use 844-666-6270 and call to confirm if it does not connect. Our Medicaid guide explains who qualifies.

What do seniors pay on Metro-North?

Riders 65 and older, people with qualifying disabilities and Medicare card holders pay half the one-way peak fare on Metro-North. The reduced fare cannot be used on weekday morning trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 am. It is fine in the evening rush.

Show a Reduced-Fare OMNY card or MetroCard, a paratransit card, a Medicare card (a Medicaid card does not count), or a license or passport. Seniors who buy on board skip the on-board surcharge. There is no reduced-fare option for multi-trip tickets such as monthlies. For a parent heading into New Jersey, the Port Jervis and Pascack Valley lines are on the other side of the Hudson. Hudson Link buses across the Hudson charge riders 60 and older $1.35, or $1.85 with a two-hour transfer to the Bee-Line or Transport of Rockland.

How do you book a first ride?

  1. Call your parent's town first. Use the table above. Ask who can ride, which days, how far ahead to call and the suggested contribution.
  2. Get the Half-Fare ID. Call 914-813-7777 for the Bee-Line reduced-fare application, or use a Medicare card on the bus.
  3. Apply for ParaTransit early. If walking to a stop is hard, call 914-995-7272, press 3, and send in the application before the need is urgent.
  4. Book medical rides by phone. For a parent 60 or older, try TRA at 914-764-3533. With Medicaid, call MAS at 844-666-6270 three days ahead.
  5. Ride along the first time. Learn the pickup spot and the timing together. Note the return time and the number to call if the ride is late.
Before the car keys go

The county's Older Driver Family Assistance Program (914-813-6188) helps families plan the talk about driving. See our guide to older drivers in New York for license rules.

faq.q: How can my mom in Yonkers get to her doctor if she stops driving?
faq.a: If she can walk to a stop, the Bee-Line costs $1.50 with a Medicare card or Half-Fare ID. If she cannot use the bus, apply for Bee-Line ParaTransit at 914-995-7272 (press 3); rides cost $5 within three quarters of a mile of a Bee-Line route. TRA gives free medical rides to adults 60 and older at 914-764-3533. You can also ask the Yonkers Office for Aging (914-963-4411) about local rides.

faq.q: Is there a senior bus for my dad in Ossining or Briarcliff Manor?
faq.a: Yes. The Ossining Senior Center runs a Wednesday 12:30 pm bus to the Croton ShopRite for seniors who eat lunch at the center first, for $2. It also sells discount taxi coupons to Ossining and Briarcliff residents 60 and older at $3 each, up to 15 a month, for use around Ossining, Briarcliff, the Croton ShopRite and Phelps Hospital. Call 914-762-1350.

faq.q: Does being over 65 qualify someone for Bee-Line ParaTransit?
faq.a: No. ParaTransit is only for people who are functionally unable to use the regular Bee-Line bus. Age alone does not qualify, and neither does a disability by itself. Riders 65 and older who can use the bus get the $1.50 reduced fare instead.

faq.q: How far ahead do I book Bee-Line ParaTransit?
faq.a: Up to 7 days ahead, by phone at 914-995-7272 (press 1), Monday to Friday, 9 am to 5 pm. Next-day trips must be booked by 5 pm. You can also book online or in the ParaTransit app. Cancel at least 2 hours before the trip.

faq.q: Can seniors use the reduced fare on Metro-North at rush hour?
faq.a: Mostly yes. The reduced fare, half the one-way peak fare for riders 65 and older, works at all times except on weekday morning trains arriving at Grand Central between 6 and 10 am. It is valid in the evening rush.

faq.q: Does Medicaid pay for rides in Westchester?
faq.a: Yes, for medical appointments. Call Medical Answering Services at 844-666-6270, or book at medanswering.com, at least 72 hours ahead. Medicaid does not pay for trips to pharmacies or grocery stores.

title: When a parent dies in New York: the first days and weeks
seoTitle: When a Parent Dies in New York: What to Do First
seoDesc: What to do when a parent dies in New York: death certificates in NYC and upstate, telling Social Security, the DMV, pensions and banks, the will and the court.
dek: The first week is mostly phone calls and paperwork, and most of it can wait a day or two. Here is what has to happen first, who to tell, and when the Surrogate's Court comes in.

body:
When a parent dies in New York, the first jobs are to choose a funeral director and order certified death certificates. Almost everything after that, from Social Security to the bank to the Surrogate's Court, runs on those certificates, so they come first.

The rest can usually wait a few days. This guide goes in the order most families actually need it: the first day, the first week, and the first month.

What has to happen in the first 24 hours?

If your mom or dad died at home in New York City, the city's guidance is to call 911. Paramedics, the NYPD or the Office of Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) will respond, and in some cases OCME lets the body go straight to a funeral home. OCME handles certain deaths, including the sudden death of a person in apparent good health, accidents and deaths that happen in a suspicious or unusual way. If your parent died in a hospital, a nursing home or on hospice, ask the staff or the hospice team what happens next.

Next, pick a funeral home. In New York State, only a licensed and registered funeral director may arrange the care, moving, preparation, burial or cremation of a person who has died, according to the state Department of Health. At the least, the funeral director files the death certificate, moves the body and works with the cemetery or crematory.

A few things are worth doing on day one if you can.

  • Look for written wishes. Your parent may have left instructions, a prepaid funeral agreement or a cemetery deed. New York lets people name an agent to control their funeral arrangements, and that agent comes before other relatives.
  • Decide who speaks for the family. The person who signs with the funeral home is the customer and is responsible for the bill. Pick one person to make the arrangements and pass along family decisions. Our funeral and burial costs guide covers the price rules and help with the bill.
  • Have the Social Security number ready. Give it to the funeral director, who usually reports the death to Social Security.
You do not have to decide everything on the first day. Choosing the funeral home is what can't wait.

How do I get death certificates, and how many?

The funeral director files the death certificate with the registrar where the death happened and can order certified copies for you. New York's Department of Health says the funeral home cannot charge more than the actual government fee for them. Where your parent died decides who issues the copies and what they cost.

Where the death happenedWho issues copiesCost per copy
The Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens or Staten IslandNYC Health Department, Office of Vital Records$15, plus $9.30 per online order, $7.50 per mail order or $2.75 in person
Anywhere else in New York StateNYS Department of Health, Vital Records, or the local registrar where the death happenedState: $30 by mail, $45 online or by phone plus a vendor fee

In the city, the Health Department calls online orders through VitalChek the fastest way, and mail orders take longer. In-person orders at the Office of Vital Records, 45 Lafayette Street in Manhattan, need an appointment. A spouse or domestic partner, parent, child, sibling, grandparent or grandchild can order a full city death certificate, and so can the informant named on it and the person in charge of the funeral. Nieces, nephews, aunts and uncles can get only the standard certificate. Call 311 with questions.

Outside the city, the state's Vital Records office says the spouse, parent, child or sibling can order. You can also go to the local registrar in the town or city where the death happened. The state's call center is 855-322-1022.

How many should we order?

Count the places that will want a certified copy, not a photocopy. A typical list includes each bank or brokerage, each life insurance company, each pension, the Surrogate's Court, and the county clerk if there is a house to sell. The state pension system, for one, needs an original certified copy before it pays a death benefit. Ordering a few extra through the funeral home at the start is usually easier than ordering more by mail later.

Who do we tell, and in what order?

Start with Social Security, because it also tells Medicare. Then move to pensions, banks and the rest. Here is the order most families work through.

  1. Social Security. The funeral home usually reports the death if you give the director your parent's Social Security number. If no funeral home reports it, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. Social Security does not take death reports online or by email. You will need the name, Social Security number, date of birth and date of death.
  2. Return the last payment. Social Security does not pay your parent for the month of death. Social Security says the benefits received for the month of death and any later months must be returned. If you aren't sure which payment that is, ask Social Security before spending it.
  3. Medicare. Social Security handles death reports for Medicare too. Call your parent's Medicare Advantage, Part D or Medigap plan separately to end coverage.
  4. Medicaid. If your parent had Medicaid, tell the office that handled the case. In New York City that is HRA. Elsewhere it is the county Department of Social Services.
  5. Pensions. For the New York State and Local Retirement System, use its online death report form or call 1-866-805-0990, then press 3 and 1. It needs an original certified death certificate before it pays any death benefit. For a private or union pension, call the plan administrator.
  6. Banks, cards and insurers. Tell each one, ask how they want proof of death, and ask whether the account names a beneficiary.
  7. The DMV. Mail a copy of the death certificate and a photocopy of the license or ID card to the DMV License Production Bureau, P.O. Box 2688 ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0668.
  8. Voter registration. The state Board of Elections says a registration is cancelled by written letter to the county board of elections, not by email. In the five boroughs, that is the NYC Board of Elections.

A surviving spouse may also qualify for monthly survivor benefits on your parent's work record. A spouse may also get a one-time $255 death payment. If there is no spouse, some children may qualify. See our Social Security guide for the current figures.

What about the car?

New York has a shortcut for one car worth $25,000 or less. Under state law it passes to the surviving spouse. If there's no spouse, it goes to children under 21. The DMV's Affidavit for Transfer of Motor Vehicle (Form MV-349.1) handles a transfer to someone else and must be notarized.

If there's more than one vehicle, or one worth more than $25,000, the cars become part of the estate. Then the executor or administrator signs the title and shows letters from the Surrogate's Court. To get back part of the registration fee, surrender the plates at a DMV office, ask for a transfer receipt, and have the executor mail Form MV-215 with "deceased" written on it.

How do we protect the home and the money?

An empty house or apartment is a target, and so is a dead person's identity. A few steps in the first week help.

  • Lock up. Collect keys, check that doors and windows lock, and put valuables and papers somewhere safe.
  • Keep the bills paid. Keep heat, power and insurance going, especially in a house upstate in winter. Tell the homeowner's insurer the house is vacant, because some policies change when no one lives there.
  • Forward the mail. The mail tells you about accounts you didn't know existed.
  • Stop using your parent's money. Under state law, a power of attorney ends when the person who signed it dies. After that, accounts in your parent's name alone generally wait for the person the Surrogate's Court appoints.
  • Keep every receipt. Funeral costs and bills you pay may be repaid from the estate later.

If your parent rented in New York City, look at the lease and talk with the landlord before you clear the apartment. Ask how much time the family has.

Where is the will, and what if we can't find it?

Look first in your parent's papers, then ask the lawyer who drafted it. If you find the original signed will, keep it somewhere safe and don't take it apart. Our probate guide covers what the court asks for.

Two less obvious places are worth checking.

  • The Surrogate's Court itself. New York lets people deposit a will with the Surrogate's Court of their county for safekeeping. After death, the court opens it and files it. Call the Surrogate's Court in your parent's county and ask whether a will is on deposit.
  • A safe deposit box. If the box was in your parent's name alone, the bank won't simply open it for you. Under section 2003 of the Surrogate's Court Procedure Act, the court can order the bank to let a named person look inside for a will, a cemetery deed or a life insurance policy. The filing fee for that petition is $20. A joint renter on the box, or a deputy your parent had named, can look for burial instructions or a cemetery deed without a court order, with a bank officer present.

When do we need the Surrogate's Court?

You need the court when your parent owned property in their name alone that doesn't pass to a named beneficiary. Accounts with a payable-on-death beneficiary, life insurance, retirement accounts, and property owned jointly with right of survivorship usually go straight to the named person.

SituationWhat usually applies
Will, plus property in the parent's name aloneProbate in the Surrogate's Court
No will, plus property in the parent's name aloneAdministration in the Surrogate's Court
Personal property of $50,000 or less and no real estate in the parent's name aloneSmall estate (voluntary administration)
Everything passed by beneficiary or joint ownershipOften no court case at all

The small estate limit comes from section 1301 of the Surrogate's Court Procedure Act. It covers personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting property that state law (EPTL 5-3.1) sets aside for a surviving spouse or children under 21. Personal property means bank accounts, stocks, cars and the like, not the house.

For a bigger estate, court filing fees run from $45 to $1,250 depending on value. You file in the county where your parent was domiciled, which is usually where they lived. In the city each borough has its own Surrogate's Court, so a parent who lived in Riverdale files in Bronx County, and one in Bay Ridge files in Kings County. Our probate guide walks through each proceeding step by step.

Will Medicaid make a claim?

Possibly. If your parent was over age 55 or permanently in a nursing home or other institution, federal and state law require New York's Office of the Medicaid Inspector General to seek repayment of certain Medicaid costs from the estate. The claim is against assets in your parent's name only. Family members are not personally responsible for it, and recovery is put off while a spouse, a child under 21 or a blind or disabled child survives. See our Medicaid guide for how the program works.

Does New York estate tax apply?

For most families, no. New York's estate tax applies only when the estate is larger than the basic exclusion amount, which is $7,350,000 for deaths in 2026, according to the state Tax Department. If it does apply, the executor must file Form ET-706 and pay within nine months of death.

Count the house at today's value, not what your parents paid. A long-held home in Westchester, on Long Island or in Brooklyn can push an estate higher than families expect. Read our New York estate tax guide if the total is anywhere near the line.

A simple first-month list

Certified death certificates ordered. Social Security told. Pension and insurers called. DMV letter mailed. House secured and insured. Will found, or the court asked. A list of every account and who it names. With that list you can tell which court process, if any, you need.

Our power of attorney guide explains why those papers stop working at death and what replaces them.

faq.q: How do I get my dad's death certificate in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Ask the funeral director to order certified copies when you make arrangements. You can also order from the NYC Health Department through VitalChek online, by mail or in person at 45 Lafayette Street by appointment. Each copy costs $15 plus a processing fee: $9.30 online, $7.50 by mail or $2.75 in person.

faq.q: My mom died in Albany. Who do I tell first?
faq.a: Choose a funeral home and give the director her Social Security number so it can report the death to Social Security, which also tells Medicare. Then call her pension, banks and insurers, and mail a copy of the death certificate to the DMV. If she had Medicaid, tell the Albany County Department of Social Services.

faq.q: Can I report a death to Social Security online?
faq.a: No. Social Security accepts death reports by phone or in person only. Usually the funeral home reports it. If not, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.

faq.q: Do we have to return my father's last Social Security payment?
faq.a: Yes, if it was for the month he died. Social Security says benefits received for the month of death and any later months must be returned. If you aren't sure which payment that covers, ask Social Security.

faq.q: What is the small estate limit in New York?
faq.a: Personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting property set aside by law for a surviving spouse or children under 21. Real estate in the parent's name alone means you need probate or administration instead.

faq.q: How much do death certificates cost outside New York City?
faq.a: From the NYS Department of Health, $30 a copy by mail or $45 a copy online or by phone, plus a vendor fee per order. You can also order from the local registrar where the death happened.
